docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Case management: He follows Local Rule 16.1(D) for the initial scheduling conference and doesn’t ask about settlement that early, but he schedules mediation unless the parties refuse. At the conference he sets summary judgment motions within 9 months, the final pretrial conference within 11 months, and trial within 12 months. He holds no status conferences unless a party asks.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Discovery: He typically decides discovery motions himself, on the papers, with no hearing except in extremely rare cases, and adds no requirements beyond Local Rule 37.1(A). He will consider an emergency discovery motion, but calling it an emergency doesn’t make it one. General protective orders are encouraged, but he disfavors using them to address sealed filings. No expert may testify to anything not fully set out in the expert’s report. Daubert motions should be decided before discovery closes.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Beyond the Local Rule 7.1(b) page limits he adds no requirements. He welcomes reply and sur-reply briefs with no page limit and doesn’t wait for them before ruling. He wants a courtesy copy if exhibits are voluminous. He typically holds hearings on motions to dismiss and on summary judgment, usually giving each side no more than 10 minutes, or 5 for simple motions. Post-argument briefs are welcome but won’t hold up his ruling.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Trial: Proposed voir dire, jury instructions, witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine are due at the latest on the Friday before Monday’s empanelment. Motions in limine are limited to 20 pages. Exhibits are numbered when in evidence, without regard to which party offers them, and letters are used for identification, running A to Z, then AA, AB, AC. Trial days run 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. He generally allows 15 minutes per side for openings and 30 for closings, and he keeps time. He seats 12 civil jurors and doesn’t allow attorney voir dire.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: He handles criminal discovery himself, usually on the papers, and sets a tentative trial date at the initial conference. Release motions go first to the magistrate judge. He typically holds a hearing on a motion to review a detention order. Sentencing memoranda are welcome but not required, and he wants them early enough to read.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Posted orders: His page posts a standing order on interim CJA 20 vouchers in excess-compensation cases and a scheduling order for the initial conference, which adds topics beyond Local Rule 16.1(D). I didn’t read those files here, so read them before the conference.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Case management: He wants copies of the litigants’ signatures on the Local Rule 16.1 certificates, not electronic signatures, though original signatures aren’t needed to file. He tries to schedule mediation after fact discovery but doesn’t require it. At the initial conference he sets the whole schedule, including the final pretrial conference and trial, and he rarely holds status conferences.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Discovery: He tells counsel most discovery motions are unnecessary and warns that obstructive lawyers may be sanctioned. He usually refers discovery motions to the magistrate judge, without a hearing. A protective order must say it is subject to Local Rule 7.2. He doesn’t schedule Daubert motions, and most that are filed are denied.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Usually no reply brief without leave of court, granted only for good cause and capped at 10 pages. He requires no courtesy copies of exhibits. He holds hearings on motions to dismiss only sometimes, and on summary judgment only when an issue isn’t sufficiently briefed, usually allowing 15 minutes per side. Post-argument briefs are rare.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Trial: Motions in limine are limited to 10 pages and are usually due two or three weeks before trial, along with requested jury instructions, voir dire questions, and objections to the other side’s witness and exhibit lists. He wants paper copies of those in chambers. Exhibits are marked in one numbered sequence, not as “government” or “defendant” exhibits. He sets time limits for openings, evidence, and closings after consulting counsel. Counsel can’t wander the courtroom, may use a movable podium or none, and sidebars are allowed only when absolutely necessary. In bench trials, proposed findings and conclusions are due before trial.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: He leaves criminal pretrial matters to the magistrate judge, including release motions, and decides suppression motions on the papers unless a hearing is warranted. A sentencing memorandum isn’t required but is strongly advised.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Remote proceedings
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Remote proceedings: As of Fall 2022 he routinely held no events by Zoom in civil or criminal cases, but would consider it for good cause. His page says there are no COVID-19-related restrictions in his session.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Posted orders: His page posts seven form orders: a notice of the initial scheduling conference with an order for the joint statement and electronic filing, a scheduling order, notices setting civil and criminal jury trials, a notice of initial pretrial conference, an order regulating non-jury civil trials, and a notice of a Rule 11 hearing. I read the first three and the civil jury trial order here. The other four are posted but I didn’t read them.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Initial scheduling conference
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Initial scheduling conference: His notice treats attendance by the senior lawyers ultimately responsible for the case, and compliance with Local Rule 16.1(B), (C) and (D), as of the utmost importance. A continuance is allowed only if counsel is actually engaged in trial, and noncompliance can bring sanctions under Local Rule 1.3. Initial disclosures under Local Rule 26.2(A) are due within two weeks after the conference, and no formal discovery can start until you comply. Plaintiff’s counsel must notify any party who hasn’t appeared. All future filings must be made electronically unless he grants leave for good cause, and notices and orders go out only by email.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Newer lawyers
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Newer lawyers: His session strongly encourages relatively inexperienced attorneys to take part in all proceedings, including summary judgment arguments and witness examinations. They must be fully prepared and have authority fitting the proceeding, and in an evidentiary hearing of substantial complexity, such as examining a witness at trial, they must be supervised by a more experienced lawyer unless he allows otherwise.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Scheduling order
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Scheduling order: After the conference the order sets deadlines to amend pleadings, designate experts and make their disclosures, finish expert depositions, finish discovery, and file summary judgment motions. Responses to summary judgment are due 14 days later under Local Rule 7.1, and filings must conform to Local Rule 56.1. A further status conference follows, with a joint status report due seven days before. Changes need a motion showing good cause, with affidavits or record references, the reasons, what discovery remains, and a date certain for finishing.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Civil jury trial
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Civil jury trial: Trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. until deliberations. A pretrial conference is set about three weeks before trial, attended by trial counsel with settlement authority. A pretrial memorandum is due seven days before that conference, extended only for exceptional cause, and failing to file it can mean dismissal, default or other sanctions. At the same time, file separately your requested jury instructions with authority, any proposed special verdict forms, proposed voir dire questions, and motions in limine. By the first day of trial, before the jury is impaneled, file exhibit lists in his format: undisputed exhibits in one numbered sequence, and contested items in one capital-letter sequence, regardless of which party offers them. During deliberations counsel may leave the courtroom but must be back within 5 minutes of a call from the depu

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Posted orders: Courtesy copies (2006 order): file a paper courtesy copy, stamped “Courtesy Copy: DO NOT SCAN,” of any electronic document relating to a dispositive motion, opposition, reply or sur-reply, with all exhibits. Her order counts motions to dismiss, summary judgment, suppression, preliminary relief, judgment as a matter of law, Daubert motions and motions in limine as dispositive for this purpose. Sealing (2015 order): she generally denies motions to seal whole memoranda and attachments, because filings are presumed open. Redact the public filing and seek to seal only truly confidential material, with a supporting affidavit from a person explaining the need. A party’s agreement or a protective-order designation isn’t enough. If the dispute can’t be resolved, file the full memorandum under seal, then a redacted public version within 7 working days

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Case management: At the initial scheduling conference she schedules fact discovery, expert discovery, Daubert briefing, summary judgment briefing, trial and mediation. Counsel should be ready to discuss the facts and legal issues and the amount of discovery needed for settlement. She asks about proportionality and wants to hear if a protective order dispute is likely. Status conferences are rare and only at the lawyers’ request. Don’t assume a continuance will be granted, and last-minute requests short of a true emergency are disfavored.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Discovery: She typically refers discovery motions to the magistrate judge, without a hearing. A protective order doesn’t bind her, and she independently decides what is public in her opinions and filings. Daubert motions are scheduled at the initial conference and shouldn’t be filed as motions in limine just before trial.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: She likes reply and sur-reply briefs, within the 20-page limit under the local rules, but will strike “supplemental” replies. She typically holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment, with time limits set as needed. She allows parties to bring new case law to her attention afterward.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Trial: She typically requires a trial brief in civil and criminal cases, sometimes waived if summary judgment briefing was extensive. In civil cases the joint pretrial memorandum and individual trial briefs are due seven days before the final pretrial conference. Deadlines for voir dire, instructions and motions in limine are set at the pretrial conference. Number agreed exhibits and letter contested ones, using her exhibit-list templates. Bring a courtesy copy of trial exhibits in a binder at trial. Counsel must resolve deposition objections before trial and present any that remain so the Court has at least 3 business days to rule. She seats 10 civil jurors, and in bench trials likes proposed findings before trial, supplemented within two weeks after.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: She holds an initial pretrial conference at the close of discovery to complete the pretrial order and set a trial date, always holds a hearing on suppression motions, and resolves release motions herself. A sentencing memorandum is required when the guidelines are disputed or a variance or departure is sought.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Remote proceedings
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Remote proceedings: As of Fall 2022 she typically held Rule 16 conferences, status conferences and non-complex dispositive motion hearings by Zoom, and held criminal trials, pretrials, revocations, sentencings and evidentiary hearings in person. She would consider Zoom for other events on request for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Michael Ponsor (D. Mass.) — Mediation order
docs.x: Judge Michael Ponsor, D. Mass.. Mediation order: His page posts one form order, on mediation. Mediation is held by video conference, and lawyers must attend with clients or representatives who have authority to negotiate and commit to settlement terms. Everyone participates in good faith, and all communications stay confidential. Each party gives the court, five days before, a confidential settlement memorandum of no more than five pages: the background and key issues with a breakdown of claimed damages, the strongest and weakest points in each side’s case, and the status of negotiations including each side’s last proposal. Counsel confer first to confirm where settlement proposals stand. The memoranda go by email to the courtroom deputy, are not docketed or shared with the other side, and are returned afterward. If a party thinks the case isn’t ready for mediation, it must say so in wri

docs.t: Judge Michael Ponsor (D. Mass.) — Other practices
docs.x: Judge Michael Ponsor, D. Mass.. Other practices: His page posts no other standing orders and no Judicial Forum Survey answers, so check with chambers for scheduling and motion practice.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Posted orders: His page posts one form notice of the initial scheduling conference. It treats attendance by the senior lawyers ultimately responsible for the case, and compliance with Local Rule 16.1(B), (C) and (D) (and 16.6 in patent cases), as of the utmost importance. A continuance is allowed only if counsel is actually engaged in trial, and noncompliance can bring sanctions under Local Rule 1.3. Plaintiff’s counsel must notify any party who hasn’t appeared.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Case management: Normally he sets only the fact discovery schedule at the initial conference and schedules a status conference before fact discovery ends, where he may take up discovery, the schedule, mediation (especially the court-annexed program) and any problems. He generally makes only a general inquiry about settlement. Where e-discovery matters, parties usually negotiate a protocol.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Discovery: He has no typical practice on who decides discovery motions: he refers some to the magistrate judge and decides others himself, and typically holds no hearing. He strictly enforces the time periods in Civil Rule 26, Criminal Rule 16 and Local Rule 116.1 for expert disclosures. A protective order must provide that any later amendment needs the court’s approval. “Emergency” discovery disputes should be rare. With a pro se party he may waive the Local Rule 7.1 consultation requirement.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: He allows reply and sur-reply briefs without a usual page limit, but expects them to be succinct and targeted. For motions with lengthy memoranda or supporting materials he will often ask for courtesy paper copies. He holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment most of the time, with no usual time limits on argument. Post-argument briefs depend on the circumstances, for example a new issue raised at argument.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Criminal matters: Criminal discovery is ordinarily handled by the magistrate judge during pretrial supervision, who also sets the deadline for suppression motions. A release motion goes first to the magistrate judge, and he typically holds a hearing on a motion to review a detention order. A sentencing memorandum isn’t required but is useful, and the government must give advance notice that victim statements will be offered. He answered none of the trial-practice questions in the survey.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Sealing and protective orders (Aug. 6, 2025)
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Sealing and protective orders (Aug. 6, 2025): He generally denies motions to seal whole memoranda and attachments, because filings are presumed open and only compelling reasons justify sealing. Instead, file a redacted public version as an attachment to a motion to file the unredacted document under seal. The motion must follow Local Rule 7.2 and be supported by an affidavit that identifies each redaction by page number and justifies it. It must describe generally what is to be sealed, how long, and the legal grounds. Anyone may oppose within 7 days. If granted, within 7 days file the unredacted version under seal, file the redacted version publicly, and serve the unredacted one on all parties. The parties’ agreement to a confidentiality designation, or a discovery order limiting disclosure, isn’t enough by itself. If you can’t confer or you disagree, co

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Default judgment (Feb. 2, 2026)
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Default judgment (Feb. 2, 2026): A default judgment motion must comply with Rule 55, including affidavits on the damages sought, the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, and that no defaulting party is a minor or incompetent. For a sum certain, also submit a form of order like his Appendix A within 14 days after the motion. For any other amount, submit supporting affidavits within 14 days. The defaulting party may file a substantiated opposition and ask for a hearing within that 14 days, and he takes the motion up on the papers afterward. A noncompliant motion may be denied, with renewal barred for six months and no interest, costs or fees added after the original motion. File the motion within 30 days of the clerk’s order pointing you to this standing order, or file an affidavit showing good cause, or risk dismissal for want of prosecution.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Case management: He usually sends a standard order with a scheduling template that follows Local Rule 16.1. He asks the parties about mediation, and often checks in after fact discovery and before expert expenses. Where ESI is significant, counsel should have a plan, especially if the parties’ ESI capabilities are very unequal. He invites the parties to propose expert deadlines at the outset.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Discovery: He holds a hearing on a discovery dispute if he has open questions after reading the submissions, and often requires or encourages an informal conference under his supervision as part of the Local Rule 37.1 conferral. For bottlenecks, parties can contact his courtroom deputy to arrange a brief phone or Zoom hearing.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Reply briefs are allowed up to 12 pages, due 7 days after the opposition. For a sur-reply, file a motion for leave and attach the proposed submission. He usually holds hearings on motions to dismiss and always on summary judgment, with no fixed time limits, and may ask for supplemental briefing on open questions. No courtesy copies are required.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Mediation: He has a standard pre-mediation order and expects the parties to follow it. He strongly prefers in-person mediation, requires the parties to attend, and discourages trial-style opening statements.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters and Zoom
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Criminal matters and Zoom: He will generally postpone or cancel an interim status conference on a joint request, if the parties file a joint status report with a clear update and next steps and represent that all parties agree to exclude time until the next conference. As of Fall 2022, civil status conferences were commonly held by Zoom, and he would consider Zoom for other events when safety or cost warrant.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Protective orders (Sept. 20, 2021)
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Protective orders (Sept. 20, 2021): Any proposed stipulated protective order must include her provision: nothing confidential gets filed until you obtain a ruling on a motion to impound under Local Rule 7.2, and the parties’ confidentiality designations don’t bind the Court. A party sealing its own material must give specific reasons. Before filing another party’s confidential material, confer with the designating party. If you can’t agree, the filing party moves to seal and the designating party must file a supporting statement within two weeks. File redacted versions on the public docket and send unredacted courtesy copies to the Clerk’s Office marked NOT FOR DOCKETING – COURTESY COPY – SEALED FILING. She encourages use of the court’s model protective order, attached to her order, and wants a proposed order filed as soon as practicable.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Summary judgment briefing (Dec. 15, 2021)
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Summary judgment briefing (Dec. 15, 2021): This order applies to consent cases before her. A reply is allowed within 7 days after the opposition, up to 12 double-spaced pages; anything longer, later, or a sur-reply needs leave. For cross-motions the order sets a sequence: plaintiff’s motion (20 pages), defendant’s combined opposition and cross-motion within 30 days (30 pages), plaintiff’s combined reply and opposition within 21 days (20 pages), and defendant’s combined reply and sur-reply within 10 days (15 pages). File one combined statement of undisputed facts, where the opposing party reprints each fact and answers beneath it, and email the deputy clerk a Word copy. File exhibits in chronological order with a descriptive table of contents, and cite exhibits already filed instead of refiling copies. Deliver courtesy copies in a tabbed binder within 2 b

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Courtesy copies (Oct. 7, 2022)
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Courtesy copies (Oct. 7, 2022): Deliver one courtesy copy to the District Court Clerk’s Office within three business days of electronic filing. Her survey answer says she requires courtesy copies of documents over 100 pages.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Other posted orders
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Other posted orders: Her page also posts scheduling orders for referral cases and for consent cases, an initial pretrial order, a standing order encouraging newer lawyers to take courtroom roles, a standing order on protective orders in criminal cases, and a defendant’s waiver of appearance at arraignment. I didn’t read those in full, so check them before you file.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Case management and discovery
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Case management and discovery: After the initial conference she sets at least the end of fact discovery and holds a status conference before fact discovery ends. She asks whether the parties want a mediation referral, and wants to hear about anything unusual in discovery. She holds hearings on discovery motions and wants specifics on relevance and burden, plus a status report if issues are narrowed beforehand. She will hear emergency discovery motions but strongly encourages the parties to work it out or agree to a stay.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: She holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment, with no time limits. Replies and sur-replies are allowed up to 12 pages. Post-argument briefs are allowed when she has an open question or the law or facts changed.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Mediation: Her pre-mediation order says: don’t contact the deputy about scheduling, file a motion to continue with several dates, bring counsel and principals with full settlement authority, and submit a confidential memorandum of no more than 5 pages by email 14 days before, marked “Confidential - Not for Docketing.” The memo covers the merits, damages, discovery status and settlement talks. She holds a Zoom conference before the mediation and prefers to mediate in person.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Trial: She requires a trial brief and sets the trial date and deadlines about three months ahead. She holds an initial pretrial conference on motions in limine, the neutral statement and voir dire. Courtesy copies of exhibits go in a binder several weeks before trial, and uncontested exhibits use one numbered sequence. After the first full day, trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. She seats 8 civil jurors, doesn’t allow attorney voir dire, and lets jurors take notebooks. She dockets a draft jury charge and discusses it with counsel.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters and Zoom
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Criminal matters and Zoom: She refers a criminal case back to the district judge when discovery is substantially complete. As of Fall 2022 she routinely held status conferences by Zoom, civil and criminal, and considered other Zoom requests case by case.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Posted orders: His page posts a civil scheduling order and a standing order encouraging newer lawyers to take courtroom roles. I didn’t read either in full, so read them before you appear.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Case management: At the initial conference he sets fact and expert discovery and doesn’t usually set a trial date then. Be ready to give the estimated number of depositions, whether expert discovery will be needed, and why the discovery period you request is necessary. He asks about the court-sponsored mediation program at every conference and holds a status conference at the close of discovery on discovery, mediation and the trial schedule. He sets a trial date at that status conference.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Discovery: A discovery motion without the Local Rule 7.1 or 37.1 certification is denied without prejudice as a matter of course. He decides after the briefs whether a hearing is needed. He bifurcates discovery when there is a Monell claim. He will hear only true emergencies. Expert designation and deposition dates are in the initial scheduling order, and he doesn’t set a Daubert schedule at the first conference.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: The summary judgment statement of material facts should be a separate document with each fact numbered. Replies and sur-replies are allowed only on motion and only to address specific points in the response, with no page limit. No courtesy copies are required. He holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment only if the motion requires, with no time limits but a request to be mindful of the court’s time. Post-argument briefs are allowed for a previously undiscussed issue raised at the hearing.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Mediation: He requires a confidential mediation statement of no more than four pages, five business days before. It covers the key issues with a breakdown of damages, each side’s strongest and weakest points, the status of negotiations with each side’s last proposal, and the settlement proposal the party thinks is fair. A party with decision-making authority must be present, and any deviation must be requested well in advance. He doesn’t usually invite opening statements and meets with the parties separately.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Trial: Proposed voir dire, instructions, exhibit and witness lists, and motions in limine are typically due one week before the pretrial conference, where he hears and resolves motions in limine. Agreed exhibits are marked by number and contested ones by letter. Trial runs Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., and he seats 8 civil jurors.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: Be ready at status conferences with an estimate of when the case can go to the district judge, trial or plea needs such as interpreters and digital equipment, and your speedy trial position. He allows phone appearances and cancels a status conference if the parties file a joint memo addressing the local rule and agree to exclude time. He refers the case back when the defendant requests trial or a plea. With a pro se party he is more likely to hold a hearing and issue written orders.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Posted orders: Her page posts a standing order on in-person proceedings during COVID-19 and a Rule 16 scheduling order. I didn’t read either in full, and the COVID order may be out of date, so confirm with chambers.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Case management: At the initial conference she sets fact and expert discovery, written and depositions, and the dispositive motion deadlines, and sets a status conference at the close of fact discovery to review discovery, interest in mediation and settlement. She explains the court’s ADR program, and wants any outstanding discovery motions raised at the conference. With a pro se party she holds more frequent interim status conferences.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Discovery: Before a discovery motion, you can call her courtroom clerk to set up a phone conference, and may file letters or joint statements beforehand. She tries to resolve as many issues as she can without motions. If a hearing is set, she orders the parties to confer first to narrow the issues, then hears argument on what’s left. She hears emergency motions when timing is the issue, such as a deposition scheduled for the next day or a looming deadline. She usually asks the parties to agree on and propose their own protective order.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Replies and sur-replies are allowed within a 5 to 8 page limit. She asks for courtesy copies only if filings are voluminous. Whether she holds a hearing on a motion to dismiss or summary judgment depends on the issues, with no time limits on argument. Post-argument submissions are welcome on new issues raised at the hearing.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Mediation: Confidential memos are due about a week before the mediation, with a phone conference five days before to confirm readiness, that an offer and counter-offer have been made, and that the necessary people will attend. The order appears on the docket when mediation is scheduled. She mediates by Zoom or in person, as the parties prefer, and wants the parties present, with exceptions in some cases.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Trial: She requires a trial brief with a witness list, expected trial length, issues of law, outstanding motions, and a synopsis of the expected evidence. She holds an initial pretrial conference, and deadlines for voir dire, instructions and motions in limine are in the trial scheduling order. She hears and usually resolves motions in limine at the final pretrial conference, and tries to resolve Daubert motions before it. Bring loose-leaf binders of exhibits to the final pretrial conference, and meet beforehand to go over exhibits. She doesn’t allow attorney voir dire. A typical trial day is 9:30 to 1:00 and 2:00 to 3:30.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters and Zoom
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Criminal matters and Zoom: She refers a criminal case back to the district judge after discovery is complete and the final status conference, or earlier for a Rule 11 hearing or on request. As of Fall 2022 she routinely held civil status conferences and motion hearings by Zoom, left it to a defendant whether to appear by Zoom in a criminal hearing, and allowed Zoom witness testimony in civil cases when the parties agree.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Discovery disputes: call first
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Discovery disputes: call first: Under his standing order you can’t just file a discovery motion. First contact his courtroom deputy, typically by email, with a summary of the issue. He then convenes a telephone conference to try to narrow or resolve it, and only if that fails may you file a discovery motion. If he holds a hearing, he uses it as a working meeting and tries to resolve each issue, often ruling orally from the bench and following with an electronic order. He considers emergency motions when an event is imminent or when one dispute must be resolved before other discovery can go forward. He urges a protective order be filed as early as practicable.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Posted orders: His page posts a sample scheduling and instruction order and a notice of and order on mediation. I didn’t read either in full, so read them before you appear.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Case management: The joint memorandum before the initial conference should include a proposed discovery plan with expert deadlines, which he generally endorses if agreed and reasonable. At the conference he sets all significant discovery phases and the dispositive motion briefing, makes sure the parties know the court’s mediation resources, and asks about ESI volume and any protocol discussions. He holds a status conference before the end of fact discovery. He bifurcates discovery when liability or the correct defendant is genuinely in question.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: He urges parties to keep to the page limits, which he sees exceeded often. Replies and sur-replies need leave but he inclines to grant it if they will help, capped at 7 pages. He asks for courtesy copies only when filings are voluminous. He usually holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment, with no hard limits but about 30 minutes per side in mind. Post-argument briefs on specific questions are usually helpful.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Mediation: Each party submits a confidential memorandum of five pages or less, with key exhibits only to help him understand the case. He starts with everyone present, then invites counsel to make short, non-argumentative introductory comments, then holds caucuses. A party with decision-making authority must at least be reachable by phone, and he strongly prefers they attend.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Trial: He requires a trial brief and holds an initial pretrial conference to discuss legal and evidentiary issues, stipulations, witness numbers and trial length. He sets the trial date at a status conference at the end of fact discovery. Voir dire, instructions, exhibit and witness lists, and motions in limine are due around the final pretrial conference, about a week before trial, where he hears and resolves motions in limine and Daubert motions. Courtesy copies of exhibits go in a binder, and exhibits must be pre-marked in a consistent logical way. He sits 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. on evidence days and 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. once deliberations begin, and seats 8 or 9 civil jurors. He doesn’t expect to allow attorney voir dire. In bench trials counsel needn’t give a jury-style opening.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters and Zoom
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Criminal matters and Zoom: The joint status memorandum is due seven days before a status conference, and when one is late he orders a responsive memorandum by the close of business that day. He refers a case back to the district judge when discovery is complete and dispositive motions are filed or scheduled. As of Fall 2022 he routinely held civil scheduling conferences and most mediations by Zoom, contested motions in person, and most criminal status conferences by Zoom.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Motion practice order (July 24, 2026)
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Motion practice order (July 24, 2026): Follow Local Rules 7.1(a)(2) and 37.1(a) on conferring, and the 20-page limit in Local Rule 7.1(b)(4), which can be exceeded only with leave. A motion to extend a deadline is granted only for good cause and must state the reasons, summarize the discovery that remains, and give a specific date for finishing discovery, joining parties, amending, or moving. File supporting papers separately from the motion, with each attachment as its own attachment whose docket text gives the exhibit number and a short title. Cite the docket as “(Docket No. ___).” A request for oral argument goes in a separate paragraph of the motion or opposition, and without a hearing she decides on the papers.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Discovery motions: confer, then request a conference
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Discovery motions: confer, then request a conference: Before any discovery hearing you must confer, with at least one personal communication such as in person, video or phone, and certify it. Before drafting a motion to compel, for a protective order, to quash, to strike discovery responses, or similar, contact the courtroom deputy and request a brief conference by Zoom. File a joint memorandum of no more than three pages, three days before the conference, outlining the disputed areas and attaching the discovery in dispute. If you still want a motion afterward, file it by the close of fact or expert discovery, whichever applies. She won’t hear disputes from discovery done after the deadline absent good cause. The motion must set out each disputed request and the response, with your position and authority after each.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: An opposition is due 14 days after service, or 21 for summary judgment. The movant may reply as of right within 7 days of the opposition, or 14 for summary judgment, up to 5 pages, and a sur-reply is not permitted. For summary judgment, state facts in a numbered list. The opponent restates each fact in order and responds beneath it, then lists additional facts continuing the numbering, and the reply follows the same format. With cross-motions, defendant files first (20 pages), plaintiff files a combined opposition and cross-motion within 30 days (30 pages), defendant files a combined reply and opposition within 21 days (15 pages), and plaintiff may reply within 14 days (5 pages). She usually holds hearings on summary judgment and decides on a case-by-case basis for motions to dismiss.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Newer lawyers
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Newer lawyers: Normally one lawyer per party argues at a hearing, but she encourages senior lawyers to let lawyers with five or fewer years of experience argue. Tell her before the hearing, and she will allow multiple lawyers to argue for that party.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Case management: Parties must consult and submit an agreed pretrial schedule no later than 7 days before the scheduling conference, addressing the topics in her sample scheduling order. She sets fact and expert discovery, dispositive motion dates, and the next status conference, and holds a status conference near the close of fact discovery. She asks whether the parties want the court’s mediation program, and if there are no dispositive motions or mediation she may set a trial date. She encourages a protective order at the earliest time.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Mediation: Her pre-mediation notice requires counsel and principals with full settlement authority to attend in person. A preliminary settlement conference is held by video, for counsel only. Each party emails a confidential memo of no more than 5 pages, five days before that conference, marked “Confidential - Not for Docketing,” covering the merits, damages with a specific breakdown, discovery status, and settlement talks. To cancel or move the mediation, file a motion with several proposed dates and email the courtroom deputy.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Trial: She requires a trial brief and holds an initial pretrial conference, setting the trial date after the joint pretrial memorandum estimates the length. She sets deadlines for voir dire, instructions and motions in limine after conferring with counsel. Courtesy copies of exhibits go in a binder and on a flash drive several weeks before trial. Exhibits get unique numbers, with no separate plaintiff or defendant numbering, groups marked with decimals such as 5.1 and 5.2, and numbers don’t change if a document is excluded. Trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., and she seats 8 civil jurors. She shares a draft charge and verdict form before the charge conference.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters and Zoom
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Criminal matters and Zoom: Joint status memoranda are due seven days before a status conference under the local rules, and she reminds parties to file them on time. She refers a case back to the district judge when discovery is complete. As of Fall 2022 she typically held status conferences by Zoom but always accommodated requests for in-person hearings, and would consider Zoom for non-evidentiary hearings.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Posted orders: His page posts no standing orders. His survey says several practices are still being worked out, and that he will note any special filing format in his pretrial procedural order.

docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Case management: At the initial conference he asks whether the parties have discussed settlement and encourages early mediation. In cases with large-scale electronic discovery he expects the parties to have a plan on production formats, timelines and search terms. He prefers parties negotiate a confidentiality agreement before seeking a protective order.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Mediation

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Trial

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Posted orders

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Discovery: She holds a hearing on discovery motions and usually rules orally from the bench. She generally considers emergency motions, and rarely bifurcates discovery, with cost a major factor.

docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Replies and sur-replies are allowed within a page limit. docs.x: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman, D. Mass.. Other practices: He answered none of the survey’s case management, discovery, motion, or trial questions, so check with chambers if you are before him on anything but mediation.

docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Case management: She follows Local Rule 16.1. Tell her about the substance of the case and likely discovery problems, and she will discuss the best way to present discovery issues, such as motions, letters, or informal conferences.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Discovery: She has no specific requirements beyond Local Rule 37.1(A), but works with counsel on whether full briefing is needed or the issue can be decided in a phone conference. She considers real emergencies and rarely rules without letting the other side respond. She schedules Daubert motions closer to trial but prefers to address them early.

docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: For summary judgment she wants one document stating the undisputed facts with the opposing party’s response. She generally allows reply briefs, which must be very short and focused, and discourages sur-replies. She holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment with no time limits, and asks for courtesy copies only on request. Post-argument briefs are possible if she requests them or to bring new cases to her attention.

docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. A decision-maker must attend, and with permission may occasionally be available by phone.

docs.t: Judge William F. Jung (M.D. Fla.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge William F. Jung, M.D. Fla.. Summary judgment: One summary judgment motion per party without leave. File a separate Statement of Undisputed Material Facts (20 pages max) after conferring to narrow disputes: numbered paragraphs, each with a pinpoint record cite (page and line for depositions), no argument, no lawyer affidavits. Stipulations need a proposed order with the dates and have no effect until approved. Proposed judgments endorsed by the other side are entered immediately; others are held 7 days for objections. docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Removal and fictitious defendants
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Removal and fictitious defendants: Removing defendants must refile all state court papers and serve the Initial Order on all parties; pending state motions must be re-noticed under L.R. 7. In diversity removals, identify and serve Doe defendants within 120 days; extensions and substitutions are sought by ex parte application, with 7 days for others to respond, addressing whether remand would follow if diversity is destroyed.

docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Scheduling conference
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Scheduling conference: Joint Rule 26(f) Report due at least 1 week before the conference, drafted by plaintiff as a single report covering items (a) through (n), including damages range, insurance, number of depositions, settlement mechanism, and trial estimate (be ready to explain over 8 court days). Exhibit A (presumptive schedule) is mandatory: proposed dates must be Mondays, trial a Tuesday. The court may decide the schedule on the papers; begin discovery early, as tight deadlines will be set. Lead trial counsel must attend. ERISA cases must address standard of review and preemption; patent cases must propose claim construction dates (N.D. Cal. patent rules); RICO plaintiffs must file a detailed RICO case statement within 20 days of that order.

docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Discovery deadlines (trap)
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Discovery deadlines (trap): Depositions must start at least 5 working days before the cut-off; interrogatories, document requests, and requests for admission must be served at least 45 days before. Stipulations allowing responses after the cut-off are approved only in extraordinary circumstances. Motions on inadequate responses must be filed within 10 days after the cut-off. Repeated resort to the court on discovery may lead to a special master at the parties’ joint expense. Amendments and joinder must be filed within 60 days of the trial order and heard within 90.

docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Motions in limine (trap): Filed at least 4 weeks before the pretrial conference, oppositions 3 weeks, replies 2 weeks; heard at the pretrial conference. Limit of 4 per side, not counting Rule 37(c)(1) and Daubert motions (state the basis in the caption title); more require an ex parte application 7 days before the due date. Deemed made and granted: exclusion of Rule 408 settlement evidence without an offer of proof outside the jury’s presence, and of undisclosed expert opinions.

docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Jury trial
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Jury trial: Meet 30 days before trial and file one packet of jury instructions, in reading order, 7 days before trial, with a WordPerfect version emailed to chambers; label joint instructions, letter alternatives (2A, 2B), and put supporting law and objections right behind each. Show changes to pattern instructions. The court gives its own initial instructions (exemplar posted). Voir dire questions at least 4 court days before trial; one-page joint statement of the case 5 days before. The page says plaintiff submits the verdict form before the close of its case in chief (the 2013 order says the first day of trial). Questionnaires are discouraged and due 30 days before trial. Trial starts at 8:30 a.m. on day one; short trials (under 10 days) run 9 a.m. to noon and 1:30 to 4:30 p.m., longer ones 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. with no lunch. Meet 10 days before trial to s

docs.t: Judge James V. Selna (C.D. Cal.) — Court trial and criminal cases
docs.x: Judge James V. Selna, C.D. Cal.. Court trial and criminal cases: Court trials: all direct testimony is by declaration, filed by the claimant’s side 20 days before trial and the defending side 13 days before; objections 5 days before trial. Witnesses then authenticate and are cross-examined. Criminal: memoranda capped at 25 pages, replies 12; Times Roman at least 14 point or Courier 12; no supplemental briefs without leave. Discovery motions require prior consultation and particulars or won’t be heard. Change of plea within 30 days of a fully executed plea agreement; government lodges witness statements in camera 5 calendar days before trial; instructions due 1 week before trial; voir dire 5 court days before. A draft sentencing memorandum is generally available 15 minutes before sentencing.

docs.t: Judge Fred W. Slaughter (C.D. Cal.) — Motion requirements (trap)

docs.x: Judge Fred W. Slaughter, C.D. Cal.. Proposed orders and chambers copies (trap): Each party filing or opposing a motion must lodge a proposed order stating the relief and a brief rationale with citations, and email it in Word, with a PDF of the main document, to FWS_Chambers@cacd.uscourts.gov. docs.t: Judge Fred W. Slaughter (C.D. Cal.) — Specific motions
docs.x: Judge Fred W. Slaughter, C.D. Cal.. Specific motions: Parties should usually agree to an amendment that cures a pleading defect rather than litigate a Rule 12 motion. Motions to amend must state the effect of the amendment and identify the page, line, and wording of each change, with a Notice of Lodging of the proposed pleading and a redline appendix. Deliver the redline to opposing counsel at least two hours before the L.R. 7-3 conference; if the draft changes, confer again. Default judgment motions are due within 14 days after default against the last defendant or resolution of all other claims, must show subject-matter and personal jurisdiction, and must include any fee and cost request (a later fee motion will be stricken absent good cause). docs.t: Judge Fred W. Slaughter (C.D. Cal.) — Ex parte applications and TROs
docs.x: Judge Fred W. Slaughter, C.D. Cal.. Ex parte applications and TROs: Only for extraordinary relief, with a showing of irreparable prejudice and that the movant is without fault or acted with excusable neglect (Mission Power). Decided on the papers; don’t set a hearing. Any opposition or notice of non-opposition is due 24 hours after receipt of the application or 24 hours after it is filed, whichever is earlier. The same deadline applies to TRO oppositions, and the court won’t rule on a TRO until at least 24 hours after service unless notice is excused or justice requires.

docs.t: Judge Fred W. Slaughter (C.D. Cal.) — Continuances and stipulations
docs.x: Judge Fred W. Slaughter, C.D. Cal.. Continuances and stipulations: Good cause only, judged by diligence and prejudice. Requests must be by stipulation, motion, or application with a declaration giving the reasons and any prior continuance requests and their outcome. Stipulations aren’t effective until approved, and every stipulation or request to alter time must propose new dates for all affected deadlines. Criminal cases: confer on new dates and email the courtroom deputy to confirm availability before filing any continuance request. Calendar conflicts: notify both judges’ courtroom deputies at least 3 days ahead and defer to the more senior judge. A “Notice of Unavailability” has no effect and should not be filed.

docs.t: Judge Fred W. Slaughter (C.D. Cal.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Fred W. Slaughter, C.D. Cal.. Sealing: Civil: follow L.R. 79-5. Justify each item under the good cause or compelling reasons standard; blanket claims or meritless requests will be denied. Meet and confer before filing an application to seal, and file a redacted public version where redaction is feasible. Criminal: e-file the application with a proposed order that includes an alternative line in case of denial, then email PDFs and a Word proposed order to FWS_Chambers@cacd.uscourts.gov with the case number and “UNDER SEAL REQUEST” in the subject. Bracket and highlight redacted portions in the unredacted copies. Use a generic cover sheet title if the real title is confidential. Non-paper exhibits go to the Clerk’s intake on USB, not CD.

docs.x: Judge Christina A. Snyder, C.D. Cal.. Hearing dates are not reserved; notice under Local Rule 7. Courtroom 8D, Los Angeles. Written tentative rulings are generally available in court on the hearing date; the courtroom opens 20 minutes before calendar call so counsel can pick them up. Direct argument to the tentative and submit on undisputed parts. Some motions are taken under submission without appearance. Civil scheduling, status, and pretrial conferences are generally Mondays at 11 a.m.; criminal status conferences Mondays at 1:30 p.m.

docs.t: Judge Josephine Staton (C.D. Cal.) — Meet and confer and specific motions
docs.x: Judge Josephine Staton, C.D. Cal.. Meet and confer and specific motions: Failure to meet and confer under L.R. 7-3 risks summary denial, and a nonmoving party that ignores timely efforts to confer risks sanctions. The rule applies equally to pro se parties. Default judgment motions must address all seven Eitel factors and the evidence supporting the requested damages or remedy, with a proposed order incorporating that analysis; noncompliant motions are stricken. docs.t: Judge Josephine Staton (C.D. Cal.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Josephine Staton, C.D. Cal.. Summary judgment (trap): Each party may file only one summary judgment motion in the case, though it need not wait for the motion cutoff. Use tabs, tables of contents, and indices to make the papers easy to absorb. The Statement of Genuine Disputes must track the movant’s statement exactly in two columns, with the movant’s fact and evidence combined in the left column and “undisputed” or “disputed” (with reasons, evidence cites, and a description of what in the evidence refutes the fact) in the right. docs.t: Judge Josephine Staton (C.D. Cal.) — Ex parte applications
docs.x: Judge Josephine Staton, C.D. Cal.. Ex parte applications: Extraordinary relief only, and the applicant must show the need is not due to its own lack of diligence. Determine the other side’s position beforehand and state it in the application or a declaration. Tell the opponent any opposition is due within 24 hours after service. No replies without leave. If you will not oppose, email the courtroom deputy as soon as possible. Applications are usually decided on the papers and almost never granted without giving the other side a chance to respond.

docs.x: Judge Josephine Staton, C.D. Cal.. Stipulations are ineffective until approved, and the court generally will not rule on “rush” stipulations to relieve parties of filing deadlines.

docs.t: Judge Josephine Staton (C.D. Cal.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Josephine Staton, C.D. Cal.. Criminal cases: Confer at least 3 days before filing any motion and say so in the notice. Put a hearing time estimate on the caption of motions and oppositions. All pretrial motions, including motions in limine, must be noticed no later than the pretrial status conference, the Friday 11 days before trial. Default expert disclosure deadlines: government 6 weeks before trial, defense 4 weeks after the government’s disclosure. Voir dire questions and any agreed indictment summary are due 4 court days before trial; joint jury instructions and verdict form 1 week before, also emailed in Word. Counsel arrive at 8:30 a.m. on day one. Sentencing position papers and any new material must be filed and served (including on the probation officer) at least two weeks before sentencing. No sentencing videos without leave for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Josephine Staton (C.D. Cal.) — Settlement, fees, and judgments
docs.x: Judge Josephine Staton, C.D. Cal.. Settlement, fees, and judgments: On settlement of all claims, the court stays the case and expects a stipulation of dismissal within 30 days; no stay for tentative settlements or settlements in principle. The court generally won’t retain jurisdiction to enforce unless the agreement is filed under seal for review. Fee motions (other than L.R. 55-3 schedule fees) need an Excel spreadsheet listing each task on its own line: date, timekeeper, description, hourly rate, time, and a formula calculating the fee. E-file it as a PDF exhibit and email the Excel file to chambers. No Rule 54(b) partial judgment without a granted motion. When all claims are resolved, the prevailing party lodges and emails a Rule 58(a) proposed judgment.

If Friday is a holiday, the matter moves to the next Friday. Courtroom 2, Riverside. Civil hearings are on Zoom by default, except motions in limine, final pretrial conferences, and trials, which are in person. To appear in person in a civil matter (or by Zoom in a criminal matter, where in person is the default), file a request 1 week before the hearing stating that counsel met and conferred under L.R. 7-3. Meet and confer (trap): Every non-dispositive motion needs a conferral certification, placed visibly in the first substantive paragraph or the final paragraph. Allow at least three business days between attempts to confer and filing, and explain specific efforts if contact failed. Rule 12(b) motions also require prior conferral and certification, to see whether amendment can avoid the motion; parties should try not to oppose timely motions to amend.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Summary judgment: MSJ and opposition: 24 pages; reply: 12 pages; sur-reply only with leave. May be filed any time before the dispositive motion deadline. Two-party cross-motions: counsel agree who moves first; the other side files one combined cross-motion/opposition, then opposition/reply, then reply. In multi-party cases with more than two movants, submit a proposed briefing schedule before filing.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Discovery disputes (trap): No opposed discovery motion until the parties meaningfully confer under FRCP 37(a)(1) and then hold a telephone or video conference with the court. To arrange it, all counsel (not staff) send a joint email to Rothstein_Chambers@dcd.uscourts.gov with a one-paragraph joint description and three available dates and time ranges, stating Eastern or Pacific Time. Raise disputes in time to finish within the discovery deadline, or the challenge may be waived. A permitted motion must quote or attach the request and objection verbatim; the losing party may be sanctioned. Give third parties notice of these procedures; if discovery is referred to a magistrate judge, contact that judge first.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Extensions and rescheduling
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Extensions and rescheduling: Extensions are discouraged and need evident good cause, even if unopposed; press of other business ordinarily isn’t enough. File at least three business days before the deadline; oppositions within two business days. Motions to reschedule a hearing: at least five business days before it, with alternative dates available to all parties, or the court picks a date.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Hearings and courtroom
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Hearings and courtroom: The court may decide any motion on the briefs and will contact the parties if it wants argument: 20 minutes per side plus 5 minutes rebuttal unless ordered otherwise. Counsel with authority to make all decisions must attend every appearance. Rise to address the court and stay at the podium unless permitted to approach.

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Courtesy copies and records
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Courtesy copies and records: No paper courtesy copies of anything, including sealed documents. Administrative records are provided electronically only, with no physical copy filed; contact the courtroom deputy for filing instructions. For audio or video exhibits, email the courtroom deputy (Natalie Wood, natalie_wood@wawd.uscourts.gov).

docs.t: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein (W.D. Wash.) — Scheduling, settlement, and contact
docs.x: Judge Barbara J. Rothstein, W.D. Wash.. Scheduling, settlement, and contact: Usually no Rule 16(b) conference; the court issues a scheduling order from the joint status report. Evaluate settlement at the outset and tell the court early if magistrate-judge mediation might help. On settlement, promptly file a notice stating how long dismissal papers will take. Chambers are in Washington, D.C.: call (202) 354-3330 or email Rothstein_Chambers@dcd.uscourts.gov, with all parties on the line or copied. Seattle courtroom: Suite 16106.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Discovery disputes: Try to resolve disputes first. For disputes that aren’t time-sensitive, use the LCR 37(a)(2) joint motion process; a unilateral, noted discovery motion is a last resort. Time-sensitive disputes: jointly email or call the courtroom deputy (Mary_Trent@wawd.uscourts.gov, (253) 882-3824) for an expedited conference, usually by phone or Zoom, with all concerned parties (LCR 7(i)). Submit a short joint statement of the dispute and each side’s position at least 24 hours ahead; it will typically be docketed. Complex legal questions may get a briefing schedule. Urgent disputes, such as mid-deposition: call the courtroom deputy to see if the judge is available, or ask for a law clerk, who can’t rule but may clarify. If unresolved, finish the deposition and raise the issue later.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Stipulated motions and protective orders (trap)
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Stipulated motions and protective orders (trap): File as a “stipulated motion,” not a “stipulation,” “agreed motion,” or “unopposed motion.” It may be noted for the day filed but won’t necessarily be signed that day. Include a proposed order and email a Word version to settleorders@wawd.uscourts.gov. Stipulated protective orders: the district’s model order is encouraged; under LCR 26(c)(2) also provide a redline showing departures from the model, which may be emailed to settleorders@wawd.uscourts.gov.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Oral argument and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Oral argument and courtesy copies: Most motions are decided without argument. The court decides whether to grant a request only after briefing is complete and will contact the parties to schedule. Courtesy copies are not required unless requested in a particular case.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Trial days and hours (trap)
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Trial days and hours (trap): Trial runs Tuesday through Friday. The courtroom opens about 8:15 a.m.; final pretrial matters at 8:30 or 8:45; the jury panel is sworn for voir dire at 9:00. Breaks about 10:30 and 3:00 (15 minutes each); lunch 12:00 to 1:30, with matters outside the jury’s presence at 1:15; recess at 4:30 p.m. Everyone must leave the courthouse by 5:00 p.m. unless court is in session; ask the courtroom deputy about leaving materials overnight.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Trial exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Trial exhibits (trap): Each party brings three tabbed binders of paper exhibits (sides marked “Clerk,” “Judge,” and “Witness”) and two thumb drives to the courtroom deputy the morning of trial, unless the deputy says otherwise. The jury may review admitted exhibits in paper and electronic form. Pre-mark every exhibit with cause number, party and exhibit number, and a blank “Admitted” line. Plaintiff numbers 001 to 499; defendant from 500. List each document once; any party may use a listed exhibit. Electronic exhibits as searchable (OCR) PDFs named like the paper ones; audio or video must play in Windows Media Player or VLC. Email a joint exhibit list in Word (auto-numbering off) to the courtroom deputy before trial. Exhibits newly admitted during trial: email the description daily, send the PDF or a thumb drive, and add paper copies with new divider

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Jury instructions: The jury is instructed twice: before openings and after the evidence. The judge’s generic preliminary set (typically Ninth Circuit Model Instructions 1.1 through 1.11 criminal; 1.1A through 1.19 civil) is handed out at the pretrial conference, need not be submitted, and objections to it are raised there. Submit agreed instructions plus each side’s disputed ones with explanations and citations (LCR 51(e), (f)) and a proposed verdict form; the latest Ninth Circuit models are preferred. File on ECF and email Word to settleorders@wawd.uscourts.gov. Final instructions are settled with counsel at the end, with an opportunity to take exceptions, and each juror gets a copy.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Voir dire and deposition designations
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Voir dire and deposition designations: The court usually gives each side 15 minutes of voir dire, and a jury is usually sworn before the noon recess. The judge has jurors introduce themselves using topics on the board, reads a joint statement of the case (the parties supply it), and asks 15 standard questions (prior knowledge, acquaintance with parties, lawyers, or witnesses, legal, insurance, or accounting employment, prior lawsuits and jury service, military service, ability to follow the law, hardship). Besides LCR 32(e) highlighting, provide a separate chart for each deposition listing page and line of the testimony and objection, with columns for the ruling (grant/deny) and reason.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Courtroom technology
docs.x: Judge Benjamin H. Settle, W.D. Wash.. Courtroom technology: If using courtroom equipment, get trained before the first day of trial, and bring your own equipment (laptops, videos, etc.) to the training to check compatibility. Questions: courtroom deputy Mary Trent, (253) 882-3824.

docs.t: Judge Benjamin H. Settle (W.D. Wash.) — Contact

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Noting dates (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Noting dates (trap): Put the noting date in the caption and note on a weekday that is not a legal holiday. Same-day motions: stipulated, joint, or agreed motions; over-length requests; reconsideration; joint submissions; mediator appointment; default and default judgment; ex parte; recusal; and TROs. Per the posted sheet: motions for relief from a deadline and for protective orders are noted 14 days out (opposition 9 days, reply 14 days after filing); most other motions 21 days out (opposition 15, reply 21); dispositive motions, preliminary injunctions, Daubert motions, class certification, and forum changes (remand, transfer, arbitration) 28 days out (opposition 21, reply 28). The sheet is undated; check it against the current LCR 7(d). Motions in limine: note no later than 12 days before the pretrial conference. After briefing, the court decides whe

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Discovery disputes: Confer in good faith in person or by phone before seeking relief; consider the expedited joint procedure in LCR 37. Privilege logs must give enough detail to evaluate the claim; for attorney-client privilege, identify the attorney. If immediate involvement is needed, request a telephonic hearing under LCR 7(i); all counsel to the dispute must join the call to chambers at (206) 370-8930.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Default judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Default judgment (trap): Support the motion with a declaration and separately state principal, liquidated damages, pre- and post-judgment interest, and attorney’s fees, explaining how each was calculated. Provide evidence of the principal amount (attach the relevant contract portions if contract-based) and of entitlement to liquidated damages. State the interest rate and why, and for prejudgment interest the accrual date and its basis. Fee requests need a basis and a declaration from plaintiff’s counsel on the reasonable amount.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Motion form and length
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Motion form and length: The court may return over-length filings or decline to consider arguments beyond the LCR 7(e) limits. The sheet restates LCR 10 format (double spacing, 12-point text, 10-point footnotes, three inches at the top of page one).

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Sealing: Every motion to seal, including stipulated ones, must describe the documents specifically, give facts justifying sealing, and include a proposed order. Without agreement, file a properly noted motion before or with the document. Give at least 7 days’ notice before filing a document another party claims is confidential so a sealing motion can be filed with it. Tell the court what to do if sealing is denied (e.g., remove rather than unseal). Trial evidence, including confidential material, is generally public.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Mediation and settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Mediation and settlement conferences: In consent cases the judge enters an order stating whether the case is designated for LCR 39.1 mediation; the sample order sets a date to negotiate, has the parties pick and file a mediator (plaintiff applies if they can’t agree), and requires a mediator’s report. A settlement judge generally isn’t appointed until the parties have mediated. The courtroom deputy schedules the conference (Courtroom 12A, Seattle), and the court sets aside the entire day. Each trial attorney attends in person with a client or representative with full authority; failure to bring the right people or participate in good faith may draw costs and fees. Deliver a confidential memo (facts, issues, law, settlement proposal, efforts to date; helpful exhibits allowed) to chambers by 12:00 noon on the set date; don’t file or serve it.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Trial exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Trial exhibits (trap): Deliver the original and one copy of exhibits to chambers no later than the pretrial conference date, in three-ring binders with numbered tabs, each exhibit clearly marked. Plaintiff numbers from 1; defendant continues with the next unused number. Don’t list duplicates; once listed in the pretrial order any party may use an exhibit. File exhibit and witness lists and revisions. Misdemeanor trials: unless otherwise directed, give the judge exhibits in tabbed three-ring binders on the trial date. The United States numbers from 1; defendants number from 1A.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Jury selection: Civil: tell the court before trial whether the case needs an extra-large pool or individual questioning of each prospective juror, and submit proposed voir dire questions in every case. Criminal: submit proposed voir dire questions five days before trial; only Class A misdemeanor defendants get a jury in misdemeanor cases. Jurors get random numbers, and the lowest-numbered sit in the box. The court describes the case, reads witness lists, has counsel make introductions, and screens for hardship and familiarity; counsel may usually question jurors within time limits the court sets. Challenges for cause are generally heard outside the jury’s presence. Each side normally gets three peremptories, noted alternately on a court form passed back and forth (plaintiff or the United States first); excused jurors are replaced from the benches in n

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Withdrawal and criminal motions
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Withdrawal and criminal motions: Withdrawal requires leave (GR 2(g)) except for changes within the same firm: file a written motion and supporting affidavit, which may be filed under seal if it contains privileged or prejudicial information. Motions to extend time to indict or file an information must state specific facts meeting the Speedy Trial Act; boilerplate (party agreement, a speedy trial waiver, time to negotiate) is insufficient alone. A defendant seeking the extension normally files a signed waiver. The sample civil consent form is marked “Do Not Electronically File.”

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — Trial exhibits
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. Trial exhibits: Exhibits are handled electronically: admitted exhibits go to the jury through JEEPS, and DEPS is used for presentation. Counsel retrieve their own exhibits after trial.

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — New lawyers and courtroom rules
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. New lawyers and courtroom rules: The court encourages hearings conducted by lawyers practicing less than seven years, especially those who drafted the briefing; an experienced attorney may supplement their argument or questioning. Leave for supervised Rule 9 interns is freely granted, and multiple attorneys may argue for one party. Turn off mobile devices before entering. Give advance notice to use courtroom video displays. Pronouns and honorifics may be given in signature lines or to the in-court deputy.

docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. Settlement conferences (trap): On referral, the court promptly issues an order setting the date and procedures. Under the example order, persons with ultimate settlement authority must be present or readily available by phone, and any party within 100 miles of the courthouse attends in person unless excused on a written request at least one week before. Plaintiff makes a demand at least 10 days before, and defendant responds at least one week before, even if the conference is set on shorter notice. Each side emails chambers a confidential memorandum of no more than 10 double-spaced pages, without exhibits absent extraordinary circumstances, not filed or served, covering liability disputes,

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. Jury selection: The court voir dires a panel equal to the jurors to be seated (8 in most civil cases) plus all peremptory challenges; civil cases have no alternates. Sensitive issues and excuse requests are followed up with individual jurors separately via Zoom, and each panelist excused for cause is replaced before peremptories. Peremptory challenges are exercised simultaneously by written lists; overlapping strikes do not earn extra challenges, and jurors are seated from the lowest-numbered unchallenged panelist.

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — ESI and Individualized Trial Program
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. The judge encourages the LCR 39.2 Individualized Trial Program; on agreement the court sets a case management conference, and trial is held within six months of approval.

docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Filings and contact: No courtesy copies unless the court orders otherwise. Email the courtroom deputy (grant_cogswell@wawd.uscourts.gov) or whiteheadchambers@wawd.uscourts.gov, copying all counsel. No phone calls except emergencies ((206) 370-8700); no faxes.
