docs.t: Judge Steve C. Jones (N.D. Ga.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Steve C. Jones, N.D. Ga.. Summary judgment (trap): Record citations must appear in the brief itself, not only in the statement of facts: after each evidentiary reference, cite the paragraph, page, or transcript line and the paragraph number of the statement of material facts. Noncompliance can require refiling. A response to a statement of material facts must copy each numbered statement and respond immediately after it, in text-searchable PDF; nonconforming statements will be returned for revision.

docs.t: Judge Steve C. Jones (N.D. Ga.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Steve C. Jones, N.D. Ga.. Sealing: The court generally seals only items listed in Standing Order 04-02. Material marked “CONFIDENTIAL” is sealed only on a motion showing very good cause, after notice to the opposing party, under Appendix H, Section II(J); the court seals or allows redaction of only the specific confidential portions, not whole documents. Pro se parties must file sealing motions manually at the Clerk’s Office.

docs.t: Judge Steve C. Jones (N.D. Ga.) — Pretrial deadlines (trap)
docs.x: Judge Steve C. Jones, N.D. Ga.. Pretrial deadlines (trap): Deposition objections must be filed in writing at least 21 calendar days before trial or are waived; counsel must confer to narrow designations and delete nonessential colloquy. Motions in limine at least 14 calendar days before trial, responses at least 7. Proposed voir dire and requests to charge at least 7 calendar days before trial, with the charges also emailed in Word to Ms. Wright the same day. Pretrial conference in every case noticed for trial; in civil cases only attorneys attend, and must identify case-in-chief witnesses and may have to bring exhibits. A trial outline issues when the case is noticed for trial.

docs.t: Judge Steve C. Jones (N.D. Ga.) — Jury selection and trial
docs.x: Judge Steve C. Jones, N.D. Ga.. Jury selection and trial: The court asks qualifying questions and has jurors answer a printed questionnaire aloud; attorneys then get 30 minutes per side per panel for approved questions. Cause challenges are heard after all questioning, followed by a 15-minute break before strikes. Civil: 8 jurors for trials of a week or less, more for longer trials, and no alternates. Criminal: 12 jurors and 2 alternates; request more at the start of trial. Number exhibits separately and sequentially, not by category; exhibit notebooks are ordinarily provided on day one. Ask permission before approaching a witness or the bench, and raise matters outside the jury’s presence during breaks or before the day starts.

docs.t: Judge Steve C. Jones (N.D. Ga.) — Jury charges and criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Steve C. Jones, N.D. Ga.. Jury charges and criminal cases: Submit a single unified set: agreed charges first, then disputed ones showing the proponent, the legal basis, and the opposing party’s basis. Use the latest Eleventh Circuit pattern instructions, then O’Malley, and the applicable state pattern instruction for state law; do not assume the court has its own substantive charge. Sentencing memoranda must be filed at least 48 hours before sentencing. A defendant must attend the criminal pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson (N.D. Ga.) — Certificate of compliance and AI disclosure (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson, N.D. Ga.. Certificate of compliance and AI disclosure (trap): Within 7 days after the Guidelines are entered in a case, lead counsel for each party and any pro se party must sign and file a Certificate of Compliance in the attached form. Noncompliant filings may be rejected or denied. Anyone who used AI in any way to prepare a filing or submission must sign and file a Disclosure of Use of Artificial Intelligence naming the tool and certifying independent review under Rule 11, in the wording the Guidelines prescribe. Fake AI-generated case citations are unacceptable, and violations may draw sanctions up to dismissal or default judgment.

docs.t: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson (N.D. Ga.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson, N.D. Ga.. Discovery disputes (trap): No discovery motions (to compel, for protective order, or for sanctions) without prior leave. Parties must first meet and confer in person; letters or phone calls do not satisfy the duty unless repeated in-person attempts fail because of the other side. Then file a joint “Notice of Discovery Dispute” on CM/ECF and email the courtroom deputy (no argument in the email). Page limits: 5 pages for 4 or fewer issues, 10 pages for 5 to 10 issues, and 12 pages for more than 10, organized issue by issue with each side’s position. Attach only excerpts of the disputed requests and responses; no other exhibits, including emails, without approval. The court decides on the papers or holds a recorded conference. Obstruction or coaching at a deposition should be raised by a prompt conference call through the deputy rather than a later motion

docs.t: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson (N.D. Ga.) — Discovery limits and objections (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson, N.D. Ga.. Discovery limits and objections (trap): Absent prior approval, each side is limited to 25 requests for production and 25 requests for admission. Produced documents must be Bates-numbered and tied to the requests. Video or audio footage of the subject of the dispute (e.g., body camera, surveillance, cell phone video) must be produced with initial disclosures or within 14 days after discovery of it. Initial disclosures may not be reserved for later supplementation. Boilerplate and general objections are disregarded; object specifically to each request, and say whether a response given “subject to” objections is complete. Generalized cross-references (such as to a deposition) are not acceptable interrogatory answers. A pre-answer Rule 12 motion or motion to compel arbitration stays discovery and LR 16 obligations until ruled on. The judge encourages an in

docs.t: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson (N.D. Ga.) — Extensions and page limits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson, N.D. Ga.. Extensions and page limits (trap): Parties may not stipulate to extensions or extra pages; file a motion before the deadline explaining the unforeseen circumstances, with a timetable, and note any opposition. Extensions are not granted as a matter of course, even by consent. Motions to extend discovery must be filed before the period expires and state: the original and current dates, prior requests and their outcomes, the opponent’s position and reasons, discovery taken so far, why more time is needed, and a timetable. Private agreements to extend discovery are not enforced. Page-limit extension motions are due at least 5 days before the filing deadline; one filed with the brief is denied, and overlong filings may be rejected. Objections to a magistrate judge’s R&R and responses are limited to 15 pages.

docs.t: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson (N.D. Ga.) — Motions practice
docs.x: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson, N.D. Ga.. Motions practice: Title briefs on CM/ECF as “Brief in Support of …,” “Response in Opposition to …,” “Reply in Support of …,” and (only with leave) “Surreply to ….” Label exhibits by content (e.g., “Ex. 1 – Smith Deposition”); with more than 25 exhibits, file a summary chart listing each with its docket number. Bluebook citations go in the text, not footnotes; noncompliant filings may be rejected. Consent, unopposed, and joint motions must attach a proposed order. TRO or injunction requests need a separate motion with evidence. An amended complaint filed as of right in response to a motion to dismiss moots any pending Rule 12 motion or request for preliminary injunctive relief. Motions are usually decided without argument; a request on a contested substantive motion will be granted if a lawyer less than 5 years out of law school will argue.

docs.t: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson (N.D. Ga.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson, N.D. Ga.. Summary judgment (trap): Statements of material facts are limited to 50 facts, with no subparts, absent approval. Before filing the brief, file the complete transcript of each cited deposition on the docket; do not attach transcripts to the brief. Record citations belong in the brief itself, with docket numbers where possible and page and line for depositions. Responses to a statement of facts must copy each numbered statement and respond immediately after it; replies copy the statement and response. File text-searchable PDFs.

docs.t: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson (N.D. Ga.) — Chambers contact and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson, N.D. Ga.. Chambers contact and courtesy copies: Courtroom Deputy Uzma Wiggins is the main contact, by email (TRJ_CRD@gand.uscourts.gov) or in writing. Do not discuss the merits with chambers or ask when a motion will be ruled on; no ex parte communications. No courtesy copies unless requested; if requested, hand-deliver single-sided copies printed from CM/ECF with the blue header to Room 2142. Daily or rough-draft transcripts require contacting chambers at least 2 weeks before the proceeding. Leaves of absence must be e-filed; mailed copies are not considered.

docs.t: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson (N.D. Ga.) — Sealing and protective orders
docs.x: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson, N.D. Ga.. Sealing and protective orders: The court disfavors broad confidentiality designations and will not approve consent protective orders that conflict with its sealing views. Material is ordinarily confidential only if it is a trade secret, personal identifying information, or HIPAA-protected health information; over-designation may be sanctioned. Protective orders must include the Guidelines’ required paragraph tying confidential status in court filings to the court’s Procedures for Electronic Filing Under Seal. Before moving to seal, consult the designating party about less restrictive options; seal or redact only specific portions, and expect no sealing of material used in open court absent extraordinary circumstances.

docs.t: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson (N.D. Ga.) — Pretrial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson, N.D. Ga.. Pretrial (trap): Motions in limine are due at least 14 days before the pretrial conference and oppositions at least 7 days before. Plaintiff’s counsel must arrange a meeting at least 10 days before the conference to discuss settlement and stipulate facts. Bring the proposed pretrial order and any outstanding motions to the conference. Daubert motions are due by the date the proposed pretrial order is filed (LR 26.2C), with oppositions 14 days later and replies 7 days after that. A Daubert hearing is often held at the pretrial conference, so challenged experts should be ready to testify. Exhibit and witness lists, on AO Form 187, must be exchanged at least 30 days before trial. A unified set of proposed jury instructions is due 3 days after the pretrial conference, with a Word copy emailed to the deputy; supplemental charges need leave. Email proposed f

docs.t: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson (N.D. Ga.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Tiffany R. Johnson, N.D. Ga.. Trial: Court usually sits 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., with 5 to 6 hours of testimony a day. Proposed voir dire is filed with the pretrial order; jurors answer a printed questionnaire, then counsel ask approved questions, with cause challenges heard at the end and a 15-minute break before strikes. One attorney per witness objects, stating only the legal basis. Exhibit notebooks for the bench are ordinarily provided on the first day; confer with the deputy beforehand. The jury is ordinarily charged before closing arguments. A court order is required to bring exhibit boxes, laptops, projectors, or other equipment into the courthouse; move at least 3 business days ahead, naming the equipment and the people bringing it. Parties generally will not be allowed personal electronics, and trial will not be delayed for technical failures.

docs.t: Judge William M. Ray II (N.D. Ga.) — Contact and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge William M. Ray II, N.D. Ga.. Courtesy copies are required only for LR 7.2(B) emergency motions and TRO or preliminary injunction motions, sent by regular mail to Ms. Lundy; courtesy copies of summary judgment motions with voluminous exhibits may be submitted. Proposed orders are required for all consent, unopposed, or joint motions. Daily or rough-draft transcripts must be requested from court reporter Geraldine Glover at least two weeks before the proceeding.

docs.t: Judge William M. Ray II (N.D. Ga.) — Oral argument (trap)
docs.x: Judge William M. Ray II, N.D. Ga.. Oral argument (trap): The court will grant a request for oral argument on a contested, substantive motion if the request states that a lawyer less than seven years out of law school will argue at least one substantial issue. Motions to dismiss and for summary judgment will be noticed for hearing at least 45 days after filing. If an amended pleading moots a motion, docket a “Withdrawal of Motion.”

docs.t: Judge William M. Ray II (N.D. Ga.) — One-motion limits (trap)
docs.x: Judge William M. Ray II, N.D. Ga.. One-motion limits (trap): Without leave, no party may file more than one motion to dismiss (a new one is allowed after an amended complaint), and defendants with the same counsel must file a single joint motion. Without prior leave, only one motion for summary judgment or partial summary judgment per party, and counsel representing several parties must file one motion on behalf of all of them.

docs.t: Judge William M. Ray II (N.D. Ga.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge William M. Ray II, N.D. Ga.. Summary judgment: Record citations belong in the brief, not just the statement of facts. Simultaneously file the original transcript of each deposition cited, cite page and line in the brief, and attach only the cited pages, not the whole transcript. A response to a statement of material facts must copy each numbered statement and respond immediately after it; a reply must copy both the statement and the response before replying. All in text-searchable PDF.

docs.t: Judge William M. Ray II (N.D. Ga.) — Discovery (trap)
docs.x: Judge William M. Ray II, N.D. Ga.. Discovery (trap): Boilerplate and general objections are prohibited and will be disregarded; object specifically to each request. A party that objects and then responds must say whether anything was withheld because of the objection (“subject to and without waiving” alone is not allowed). Serve requests so responses are due by the close of discovery; the court typically will not compel late-served requests. Identify experts early enough to be deposed within the period. Before any discovery motion, confer in good faith, then contact Ms. Lundy; ordinarily each side submits a 1–2 page letter, and the court rules on the letters, holds a call, or authorizes a motion. The court is usually available by phone for deposition disputes.

docs.t: Judge William M. Ray II (N.D. Ga.) — Protective orders and sealing (trap)
docs.x: Judge William M. Ray II, N.D. Ga.. Protective orders and sealing (trap): The court disfavors consent confidentiality orders; ordinarily only trade secrets, personal identifying information, and HIPAA-protected health information are truly confidential. Any such order must include (and is deemed to include) the standing order’s language that confidential material submitted to the court keeps its status only by court order. To seal, e-file a motion listing the documents with a proposed order and provisionally file the documents under seal per Appendix H; send no paper copies. Tangible items go to Ms. Lundy in chambers with a proposed order.

docs.t: Judge William M. Ray II (N.D. Ga.) — Motions practice and filing format
docs.x: Judge William M. Ray II, N.D. Ga.. docs.t: Judge William M. Ray II (N.D. Ga.) — Pretrial (trap)
docs.x: Judge William M. Ray II, N.D. Ga.. Pretrial (trap): If a summary judgment motion is pending, the consolidated pretrial order is ordinarily due 30 days after the ruling unless a date is set. Plaintiffs cannot enlarge or change their claims in the pretrial order over objection. Witness and exhibit lists cannot reserve a right to supplement or adopt another party’s list; unlisted witnesses and exhibits are excluded absent manifest injustice. Motions in limine and Daubert motions at least 14 days before the pretrial conference, responses 7 days before. Proposed findings and conclusions must also be sent to the law clerk in text-searchable PDF. Anyone without a blue attorney ID card needs a proposed order, at least 3 business days ahead, to bring laptops or camera phones into the courthouse.

docs.t: Judge William M. Ray II (N.D. Ga.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge William M. Ray II, N.D. Ga.. Jury selection: Civil trials up to 2 weeks normally seat 8 jurors with no alternates (possibly 7 for trials under a week) from a panel of 20; alert the court promptly if a larger panel is needed, such as for media attention or a mutual insurer. After the court’s qualifying questions, counsel conduct general voir dire of the panel and then question each juror individually. Cause motions follow outside the jury’s presence; each side gets 3 peremptory strikes, alternating on a strike sheet starting with plaintiff.

docs.t: Judge William M. Ray II (N.D. Ga.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge William M. Ray II, N.D. Ga.. Trial: Court usually sits 9:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.; counsel present at 9:00 a.m. Expect 5 to 6 hours of testimony per day. Openings are generally limited to 20 minutes and closings to 30 minutes per side; seek more time at the pretrial conference. Before trial, give the deputy a notebook of pre-marked exhibits for the judge and file witness and numbered exhibit lists; hand the court small copies of enlarged boards. No permission is needed to approach a witness with an exhibit. Only the examining attorney may object, stating only the legal basis; one attorney per party at the charge conference. Speak from a microphone; no motions in the jury’s presence, though mistrial motions must be made immediately.

docs.t: Judge William M. Ray II (N.D. Ga.) — Jury charges
docs.x: Judge William M. Ray II, N.D. Ga.. Jury charges: File, and email to the deputy in Word, a single unified set of proposed instructions no later than the morning of the first day of trial, showing for disputed charges the proponent, the legal basis, and the opposition’s basis. Supplemental charges require oral leave and are not accepted later than a day before the end of trial absent manifest justice.

docs.t: Judge Adrienne Nelson (D. Or.) — Judge’s copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Adrienne Nelson, D. Or.. Judge’s copies (trap): Parties are exempt from Local Rule 5-10 paper filing, except for documents identified in the Trial Management Order. Do not send paper courtesy copies; the judge reads filings electronically.

docs.t: Judge Adrienne Nelson (D. Or.) — Proposed orders and jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Adrienne Nelson, D. Or.. Proposed orders and jury instructions: Submit jury instructions and proposed forms of order under LR 5 to the chambers proposed-document email address linked on the page. It may not be used for filings, and unauthorized correspondence is deleted.

docs.t: Judge Adrienne Nelson (D. Or.) — Young lawyers
docs.x: Judge Adrienne Nelson, D. Or.. Young lawyers: The judge encourages giving lawyers practicing less than 7 years substantive speaking roles, including oral argument and witness examination, especially where they drafted or significantly contributed to the briefing. An experienced attorney may supplement their argument or questioning if necessary.

docs.t: Judge Adrienne Nelson (D. Or.) — Briefs
docs.x: Judge Adrienne Nelson, D. Or.. Briefs: The court strongly encourages hyperlinking cited cases in briefs (see Section 5 of the CM/ECF User Manual).

docs.t: Judge Adrienne Nelson (D. Or.) — Expedited case management
docs.x: Judge Adrienne Nelson, D. Or.. Expedited case management: If the parties agree to an expedited trial schedule, the court will hold a case management conference on discovery limits and the need for dispositive motions, and will make every effort to set trial within six months of that conference.

docs.t: Judge Adrienne Nelson (D. Or.) — Courtroom rules
docs.x: Judge Adrienne Nelson, D. Or.. Courtroom rules: Wireless devices on silent in the courthouse. No recording at any time in the courthouse or during any remote proceeding (telephone, video, or other electronic means). Give advance notice if you need teleconferencing, the courtroom video displays, or other presentation technology. Refer to parties by their proper names (“Mr. Smith,” not “the defendant”) during argument and testimony; decorum and civility are expected.

docs.t: Judge Amy M. Baggio (D. Or.) — Judge’s copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Amy M. Baggio, D. Or.. Judge’s copies (trap): Judge Baggio expects compliance with LR 5-8(a): a fastened paper copy marked “JUDGE’S COPY,” with the Notice of Electronic Filing, delivered to the Clerk’s Office within 3 business days for dispositive and injunctive motions (and all related papers), Social Security records, and any filing over 10 pages in the aggregate. Copies with exhibits or attachments, or combined filings of 2 inches or more, go in a tabbed three-ring binder; double-sided is fine. On objections to a Findings and Recommendation, give copies of the objection and response only. For trial documents, paper judge’s copies are due at the Clerk’s Office the same day as filing, double-sided and three-hole punched; in criminal cases this applies to ALL pretrial documents regardless of length.

docs.t: Judge Amy M. Baggio (D. Or.) — Late filings and proposed orders
docs.x: Judge Amy M. Baggio, D. Or.. Late filings and proposed orders: If you file anything within 48 hours of a hearing, email the courtroom deputy to say so and/or send the deputy a courtesy copy by email. Do not file proposed orders or judgments in ECF (except protective and pretrial orders) unless the court asks; if requested, email them in Word.

docs.t: Judge Amy M. Baggio (D. Or.) — Protective orders (trap)
docs.x: Judge Amy M. Baggio, D. Or.. Protective orders (trap): Use Judge Baggio’s own modified Tier 2 stipulated protective order template, not the district’s model. Any changes require filing two versions, one clean and one with tracked edits against the judge’s template, plus an explanation of why the case needs a different approach. The judge’s template bars submitting designated material to any public generative AI tool (e.g., ChatGPT), even if anonymized. Designation disputes go first to conferral, then by email to the courtroom deputy with a one-page letter per party; the court decides whether a motion is needed. A non-designating party files designated material under seal; if it asks in writing to unseal, the designating party has 10 calendar days to move to keep it sealed or the court unseals it.

docs.t: Judge Amy M. Baggio (D. Or.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Amy M. Baggio, D. Or.. Criminal cases: Motions to continue trial are due 4 weeks before trial. Supervised release violation submissions are due from both sides 3 business days before the hearing. The USMS transport list is prepared the Monday before the next week’s hearings, so tell the court of date changes or the defendant may be transported. Contact the deputy at least 6 weeks before trial so a jury can be summoned. Parties secure their own interpreters for witnesses. 28 days before the pretrial conference, notify the deputy whether the case is going to trial; if not, set a plea hearing (plea agreement and petition due by noon the day before) or move to continue. docs.t: Judge Amy M. Baggio (D. Or.) — Criminal trial filings

docs.x: Judge Michael J. McShane, D. Or.. Scheduling: Rule 16 conferences are set after all defendants answer. docs.t: Judge Michael J. McShane (D. Or.) — Trial management order deadlines
docs.x: Judge Michael J. McShane, D. Or.. Trial management order deadlines: The court automatically enters a Trial Management Order 90 days before trial. Pretrial conferences are in person in Eugene. Under the sample TMO: 30 days before the pretrial conference, plaintiff’s exhibit lists and judge’s copies, witness statements and expert reports, special damages, and the pretrial order; 21 days before, defendant’s exhibits and witness materials, deposition designations, trial memoranda, voir dire, and verdict forms; 14 days before, motions in limine, rebuttal materials, and objections; 7 days before, responses. Trial memoranda are limited to 35 pages; all motions in limine and all responses each go in a single document not exceeding 35 pages, with separate motions as subparts.

docs.t: Judge Leslie Abrams Gardner (M.D. Ga.) — Court’s voir dire, both case types
docs.x: Judge Leslie Abrams Gardner, M.D. Ga.. Court’s voir dire, both case types: The court asks about pretrial publicity and discussion of the case, whether jurors know the judge, the parties, counsel, their firms, the listed witnesses, or other panel members, and about physical limitations that would prevent sitting through trial. It also asks about court-system employment, legal training (including paralegal, forensic, and criminal justice coursework), prior testimony, and courtroom TV shows, and whether any juror cannot follow the law as charged or sit in judgment for moral or religious reasons.

docs.t: Judge Leslie Abrams Gardner (M.D. Ga.) — Civil voir dire
docs.x: Judge Leslie Abrams Gardner, M.D. Ga.. Civil voir dire: Fill-ins cover plaintiff, defendant, each side’s attorney, and each attorney’s firm, plus a short statement of plaintiff’s claims. Civil-specific questions cover prior lawsuits (as a party or otherwise), prior jury or grand jury service, and whether any juror could not hold for the defendant if plaintiff fails its burden or could not award money damages if plaintiff meets it.

docs.t: Judge Leslie Abrams Gardner (M.D. Ga.) — Criminal voir dire
docs.x: Judge Leslie Abrams Gardner, M.D. Ga.. Criminal voir dire: Fill-ins cover the defendant, defense counsel and firm, and the assigned Assistant U.S. Attorney. Criminal-specific questions cover law enforcement and corrections employment or applications (by jurors or close family), giving greater weight to government or law enforcement witnesses, unfair treatment by the criminal justice system, and crime-prevention or neighborhood-watch membership within the last 5 years. The court instructs that the defendant need not prove innocence, produce evidence, or testify, and asks whether any juror could not follow that instruction.

docs.t: Judge Leslie Abrams Gardner (M.D. Ga.) — Witness lists for voir dire
docs.x: Judge Leslie Abrams Gardner, M.D. Ga.. Witness lists for voir dire: In both civil and criminal cases, the court reads the list of potential witnesses to the panel and asks whether anyone knows them.

docs.x: Judge Kelly Fitzgerald Pate, M.D. Ala.. Chambers contact: Courtroom 5A; chambers (334) 954-3730, patechambers@almd.uscourts.gov; courtroom deputy Kelli Fuller, (334) 954-3973. The page notes judges cannot respond to letters, emails, or other communications about pending cases.

docs.t: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr. (M.D. Ala.) — Proposed orders and courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr., M.D. Ala.. Proposed orders and courtesy copies: Submit every proposed order both as a PDF attachment to the motion and in Word by email to huffakerchambers@almd.uscourts.gov, copying all counsel. Discovery-related proposed orders (HIPAA, protective, confidentiality) go to the assigned magistrate judge’s email. Courtesy copies are not required unless ordered. If sent, they must match the CM/ECF version, be marked “Courtesy Copy,” double-sided, in a D-ring binder (unless under 50 pages), and delivered or mailed to the civil clerk’s office, Frank M. Johnson, Jr. U.S. Courthouse, One Church St., Montgomery.

docs.t: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr. (M.D. Ala.) — Motion briefing and page limits (trap)
docs.x: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr., M.D. Ala.. Motion briefing and page limits (trap): Dispositive and substantive motions (including motions to remand, to dismiss, for summary judgment, and Daubert motions): opening and opposition briefs are capped at 35 double-spaced pages and replies at 15 without advance permission. Responses are due 21 days after the motion and replies 14 days after the response; the motion is then taken under submission without notice. Non-dispositive motions: confer in good faith first, state “opposed” or “unopposed” in the caption, and summarize the conferral and areas of agreement in the first paragraph (failure is grounds for denial). Responses within 14 days, replies within 7. All submissions in 14-point Times New Roman (footnotes 12-point). Briefs over 35 pages need a table of contents, table of authorities, and delineated sections. No “letter briefs” or “letter re

docs.t: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr. (M.D. Ala.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr., M.D. Ala.. Summary judgment: Every discussion of evidence must cite page and line of the supporting deposition or document, or the point may be deemed abandoned; failing to address an argument may also be treated as abandonment. File the brief and all supporting evidence with the motion. Opponents are strongly encouraged to concede claims and arguments where appropriate.

docs.t: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr. (M.D. Ala.) — Hearings and filing cutoff (trap)
docs.x: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr., M.D. Ala.. Hearings and filing cutoff (trap): Unless an order says otherwise, all motions, briefs, and memoranda for a matter set for hearing must be e-filed by 2:00 p.m. CST the day before the hearing, or they will not be considered absent exceptional cause. The court often sets telephone conferences sua sponte; call in at least 5 minutes early. Motions to reschedule require contacting opposing counsel and good cause. Notify the court at least one day ahead if a hearing or sentencing will exceed 45 minutes.

docs.t: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr. (M.D. Ala.) — Extensions and discovery
docs.x: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr., M.D. Ala.. Extensions and discovery: Extension requests must be in writing, filed well before the deadline, and state that all counsel were timely contacted and whether they agree; noncompliant, oral, or “eleventh hour” requests are denied outright. Discovery-extension motions must list remaining discovery and discovery already done (dates served and answered, depositions taken with deponent names, and depositions requested); lack of progress may defeat the motion. The assigned magistrate judge generally handles discovery motions.

docs.t: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr. (M.D. Ala.) — Scheduling
docs.x: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr., M.D. Ala.. Scheduling: File the joint Rule 26(f) report within 30 days after all answers are filed unless the court sets another date; review the practices document and template scheduling order first. Any scheduling conference may be attended by phone. Cases are ordinarily set for a civil trial term 18 to 24 months after filing, with the pretrial conference about 28 days before the term. Per the uniform date sheets, dispositive motions are due 180 days before the pretrial conference, the discovery/settlement-conference deadline is 30 days before that, plaintiff’s experts 90 days before the discovery cutoff, and defendant’s experts 28 days after plaintiff’s. Objections to the scheduling order’s deadlines are due within 14 days of the order. Daubert motions are due with dispositive motions.

docs.t: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr. (M.D. Ala.) — Mediation and settlement (trap)
docs.x: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr., M.D. Ala.. Mediation and settlement (trap): Counsel must hold a settlement conference by the set deadline, then within 7 days file a joint status report choosing a private mediator (name and date) or a magistrate judge (four agreed dates); mediate within 45 days. Mediation is treated as mandatory absent good cause. The practices document calls this a face-to-face conference, while the template scheduling order calls for a telephone conference. Lead counsel and a representative with full settlement authority must attend mediation; report the result within 7 days. Promptly notify the court of any settlement.

docs.t: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr. (M.D. Ala.) — Pretrial
docs.x: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr., M.D. Ala.. Pretrial: Pretrial conferences are held in Courtroom 2D, Montgomery, absent order and good cause. The plaintiff emails the joint proposed pretrial order in Word to chambers 7 days before the conference. Witness lists, deposition designations (page and line; no entire depositions), and exhibit lists are due 30 days before the pretrial conference, objections 21 days before it, and replies 7 days after objections. Voir dire questions, fully briefed motions in limine, and jury instructions are due 30 days before trial; responses to motions in limine 21 days before. Avoid duplicating the district’s jury questionnaire. Trial terms last two weeks and “trial date” means jury selection.

docs.t: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr. (M.D. Ala.) — Courtroom and trial protocol (trap)
docs.x: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr., M.D. Ala.. Courtroom and trial protocol (trap): Stand when addressing the court or questioning witnesses, speak from the lectern or counsel table, and ask leave before approaching a witness each time. Address others formally. Bring the original and three copies of all exhibits in separate D-ring binders, pre-marked, with three copies of witness and exhibit lists for the courtroom deputy; for voluminous exhibits, contact the court the week before trial about electronic copies. State the legal basis for every objection; only the attorney examining a witness may object during another party’s examination of that witness. In openings and closings, stay at least 15 feet from the jury box. After-hours informal communications go to chambers email with opposing counsel copied, but they do not preserve the record.

docs.t: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr. (M.D. Ala.) — AI use
docs.x: Judge R. Austin Huffaker Jr., M.D. Ala.. AI use: AI tools are permitted but require close supervision and citation-checking; anyone who discovers fabricated citations must raise it immediately, and presenting false or hallucinated citations draws sanctions or striking of the filing.

docs.t: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon (W.D. Va.) — Motion hearings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon, W.D. Va.. Motion hearings (trap): The court does not generally schedule motion hearings; scheduling is the parties’ job. To get a hearing, contact the courtroom deputy, Kelly Anglim (Kelly_Anglim@vawd.uscourts.gov or 540-857-5117). If the parties do not promptly schedule one, the court rules without a hearing. Nondispositive motions, including motions for more time, opposed or not, may be decided at any time without awaiting a response. Dispositive motions and motions to exclude experts must be heard no later than 45 days before trial; motions in limine (including objections to deposition testimony and trial exhibits) no later than the final pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon (W.D. Va.) — Briefing and page limits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon, W.D. Va.. Briefing and page limits (trap): A supporting brief must accompany every pretrial motion unless the motion itself contains the legal argument or is certified unopposed. Oppositions are due 14 days after service of the movant’s brief (7 days for motions in limine and other trial-related motions); a late opposition means the motion is treated as unopposed, absent good cause. Replies are due 7 days after the opposition (for trial-related motions, 7 days or at least 2 days before the final pretrial conference, whichever is shorter). No surreply without prior leave. Briefs are capped at 25 pages, exclusive of exhibits, with standard margins and double spacing, unless leave is first obtained for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon (W.D. Va.) — Courtesy copies and proposed orders
docs.x: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon, W.D. Va.. Courtesy copies and proposed orders: Send a paper courtesy copy to chambers (210 Franklin Road, S.W., Suite 132, Roanoke, Virginia 24011) when a dispositive motion, with its brief and exhibits, runs 75 or more pages. Proposed orders go to Dillon.ecf@vawd.uscourts.gov as a Word attachment, copied to all opposing counsel or unrepresented parties; proposed orders filed in CM/ECF should also be emailed separately in Word.

docs.t: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon (W.D. Va.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon, W.D. Va.. Sealing: No motion, brief, or exhibit may be filed under seal except as allowed by General Local Rule 9, and a stipulated protective order or other agreement cannot modify its requirements.

docs.t: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon (W.D. Va.) — Scheduling and discovery (sample order)
docs.x: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon, W.D. Va.. Scheduling and discovery (sample order): Typical deadlines: Rule 26(f) conference 14 days from the order; initial disclosures 30 days (plaintiff) and 45 days (defendant); joinder and amendment 120 days; discovery closes 95 days before trial, with written discovery served in time for responses by the cutoff; dispositive motions and motions to exclude experts filed 80 days before trial. The parties may amend the disclosure and discovery provisions by agreement without leave but must then file a Rule 26(f) plan; changing any other deadline requires a motion and a proposed agreed order. Do not file discovery materials unless relevant to a motion or required.

docs.t: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon (W.D. Va.) — Experts
docs.x: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon, W.D. Va.. Experts: Retained-expert reports are due 90 days (plaintiff) and 60 days (defendant) before the discovery deadline. Non-retained experts (such as treating physicians) must be disclosed with Rule 26(a)(2)(C) information within 80 days (plaintiff) and 110 days (defendant) of the order; rebuttal under Rule 26(a)(2)(D). A motion to exclude an expert is due by the summary judgment deadline and is not a “motion in limine,” however titled.

docs.t: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon (W.D. Va.) — Pretrial and trial
docs.x: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon, W.D. Va.. Pretrial and trial: Trial starts at 9:00 a.m. Contact the courtroom deputy to set a final pretrial conference no later than 7 days before trial. Exchange and file witness lists (name, address, and testimony summary) and exhibit lists 28 days before trial; motions in limine are due 21 days before trial. Deposition designations 21 days before trial; counterdesignations and objections 14 days; objections to counterdesignations 7 days before trial or at least 2 days before the final pretrial conference, whichever is shorter. Parties must confer in good faith, at length if necessary, to resolve objections before the conference. Jury trials: file proposed jury instructions and special interrogatories 7 days before trial and email them in Word, with citations, to dillon.ecf@vawd.uscourts.gov; email a joint statement of the case (or separate ones if no agreem

docs.t: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon (W.D. Va.) — Settlement and dismissal (trap)
docs.x: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon, W.D. Va.. Settlement and dismissal (trap): If the case settles and the court does not receive a proposed final order within 30 days after notice of settlement, the case will be dismissed with prejudice. A party wanting the court to retain jurisdiction to enforce the settlement must move within 60 days of the dismissal order. Mediation by a magistrate judge is available on any party’s motion.

docs.t: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon (W.D. Va.) — ERISA benefits cases (trap)
docs.x: Judge Elizabeth K. Dillon, W.D. Va.. ERISA benefits cases (trap): The proposed ERISA order becomes the scheduling order unless a party objects within 10 days. Any discovery is due within 60 days, and the administrator or fiduciary must file the administrative record within 60 days. All parties are deemed to have moved for summary judgment on the record. Plaintiff’s brief (with any authenticity objections to the record) is due 30 days after service of the record, defendant’s response 30 days later, and an optional reply 7 days later. Oral argument must be requested promptly after the last brief by contacting Judicial Assistant Miriam Frazier (miriamf@vawd.uscourts.gov or 540-857-5120); otherwise the court rules on the papers. Deadlines may be moved by filed written stipulation, but no more than 60 days without leave.

docs.t: Judge Derrick Watson (D. Haw.) — Appearances and contact (trap)
docs.x: Judge Derrick Watson, D. Haw.. Appearances and contact (trap): All hearings are attended by counsel in person unless prior leave is timely sought and granted. No ex parte communication with the judge or staff about a pending case without prior leave; violations without good cause draw sanctions. Counsel may contact the courtroom manager (Tammy Kimura, 808-541-3073) about continuances and similar scheduling relief. Nothing may be faxed to chambers without prior permission from chambers staff.

docs.t: Judge Derrick Watson (D. Haw.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Derrick Watson, D. Haw.. Summary judgment (trap): Only one Rule 56 motion per party without leave, sought by noticed motion showing good cause. An early motion (for example, on immunity) followed by a later motion after more discovery is an example of good cause.

docs.t: Judge Derrick Watson (D. Haw.) — Motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Derrick Watson, D. Haw.. Motions in limine (trap): Due 3 weeks before trial; responses due 2 weeks before trial; no replies. Motions and oppositions are limited to 5 pages, and they are generally heard at the final pretrial conference. Meet and confer under Local Rule 7.8 at least 7 days before filing. No Daubert motions once trial has begun.

docs.t: Judge Derrick Watson (D. Haw.) — Electronic devices
docs.x: Judge Derrick Watson, D. Haw.. Electronic devices: In the courtroom, only attorneys of record may use devices, only for the ongoing case-related proceeding and with court approval. Phones off on entering the courtroom; no cameras or recording in the courtroom or chambers. The order does not authorize bringing devices to the courthouse for other matters. Violations draw sanctions.

docs.t: Judge Derrick Watson (D. Haw.) — Trial schedule and jury selection
docs.x: Judge Derrick Watson, D. Haw.. Trial schedule and jury selection: Jury trials run 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. with no lunch break (bring a snack); some days may run later. Jury selection days run 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. with lunch about noon to 1:30 p.m. Non-jury trials run 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., sometimes longer. The court conducts general voir dire, incorporating parties’ special questions; each side then gets a maximum of 20 minutes. Peremptories use the open, alternate-strike method on a court form. Jurors may take notes.

docs.t: Judge Derrick Watson (D. Haw.) — Exhibits and witnesses (trap)
docs.x: Judge Derrick Watson, D. Haw.. Exhibits and witnesses (trap): Meet and confer on a common exhibit set and try to stipulate to authenticity and admissibility; no statement of objections need be filed despite the Rule 16 order. File exhibit lists by the final pretrial conference date. Exhibits go in 3-ring binders no larger than 3 inches at the spine; one original and two copies are due the Thursday before trial. Disclose the next day’s witnesses to counsel and the court by 4:30 p.m. the prior business day; undisclosed witnesses may not testify.

docs.t: Judge Derrick Watson (D. Haw.) — Demonstratives and deposition testimony
docs.x: Judge Derrick Watson, D. Haw.. Demonstratives and deposition testimony: No demonstratives in opening, and no material not in evidence during examination or closing, without all parties’ consent or (failing agreement) leave of court, obtained in advance without delaying the jury. Exhibits are generally not passed among jurors. Use the microphone (lapel mics on request). For published deposition testimony, give timely notice; counsel generally meet with the court by the prior trial day to resolve objections, and the offering party provides a revised designation transcript by the start of that trial day, plus a reader if read aloud.

docs.t: Judge Derrick Watson (D. Haw.) — Jury instructions and pretrial filings
docs.x: Judge Derrick Watson, D. Haw.. Jury instructions and pretrial filings: Comply with Local Rule 51.1; L.R. 51.1(b) and (e)–(j) also apply to verdict forms. Submit instructions and verdict forms in hard copy and in Word by disk or email to watson_orders@hid.uscourts.gov. Each juror gets a copy. File a joint, brief, objective statement of the case for voir dire 2 weeks before trial. Counsel arrange their own interpreters well ahead, get advance permission for special equipment, and give the courtroom manager after-hours phone numbers before trial.

docs.t: Judge Helen W. Gillmor (D. Haw.) — Summary judgment concise statements (trap)
docs.x: Judge Helen W. Gillmor, D. Haw.. Summary judgment concise statements (trap): The separate concise statement is limited to 5 pages or 1500 words, includes only material facts absolutely necessary to the motion, and contains no argument. Facts in the moving party’s statement are deemed admitted unless controverted in the opposing concise statement. Support each fact with specific evidence, identifying the filing, the portion and page, and where it is found in ECF; highlight or otherwise emphasize the relevant portions. Documents need not be filed in full. File the concise statement separately, not as an attachment to the motion. All exhibits on originals and courtesy copies need labeled tabs. The memo attaches example moving and opposing statements (two-column facts and evidence format).

docs.t: Judge Helen W. Gillmor (D. Haw.) — Continuing trial
docs.x: Judge Helen W. Gillmor, D. Haw.. Continuing trial: All motions to continue trial filed within 30 days of the trial date are heard by Judge Gillmor.

docs.t: Judge Helen W. Gillmor (D. Haw.) — Rule 404(b) notice in criminal cases (trap)
docs.x: Judge Helen W. Gillmor, D. Haw.. Rule 404(b) notice in criminal cases (trap): Oral statements do not satisfy 404(b) notice in felony trials before Judge Gillmor. At the final pretrial conference before the magistrate judge, the government will be required to file and serve, within two days, written notice describing the 404(b) evidence with enough particularity for the defendant to identify the act. The defendant files and serves a written response within two days after the notice is filed.

docs.t: Judge Helen W. Gillmor (D. Haw.) — Trial days and out-of-jury matters
docs.x: Judge Helen W. Gillmor, D. Haw.. Trial days and out-of-jury matters: Jury trial sessions are Tuesday to Friday; in a week with a Monday holiday, Wednesday to Friday. At recesses and at the end of each session, once the jury leaves, the court asks whether counsel have matters for the record. Offers of proof, preservation of objections, motions to reconsider evidentiary rulings, and witness or scheduling discussions happen then.

docs.t: Judge Helen W. Gillmor (D. Haw.) — Objections at trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Helen W. Gillmor, D. Haw.. Objections at trial (trap): Counsel must rise and wait to be recognized before stating an objection, and state it in five words or less (for example, “Objection - Hearsay”). The court will rule, ask for a short response or explanation, or call a sidebar. No further argument in the jury’s hearing; save argument, offers of proof, and record preservation for the next recess.

docs.t: Judge Helen W. Gillmor (D. Haw.) — Courtroom decorum (trap)
docs.x: Judge Helen W. Gillmor, D. Haw.. Courtroom decorum (trap): Stand when court opens, recesses, or adjourns, when the jury enters or leaves, and when addressing or addressed by the court. Examine witnesses and give openings and closings from the lectern; approach the courtroom manager’s desk only with permission, and the bench only when invited. Address remarks to the court, refer to everyone by surname, and only one attorney per party examines or cross-examines each witness (the attorney objecting on direct handles cross). Hand unmarked papers to the courtroom manager for marking before they go to a witness, with a copy for the court, and hand offered exhibits to opposing counsel. Do not echo or thank witnesses for answers; make stipulation offers privately, not before the jury. In openings and arguments, do not express personal knowledge or opinion, read or purport to read from transcript

docs.t: Judge Helen W. Gillmor (D. Haw.) — Jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Helen W. Gillmor, D. Haw.. Jury instructions: The judge posts general civil (2023) and criminal (2023, in female and male defendant versions that differ only in pronouns) jury instructions covering standard topics such as burden of proof, credibility, experts, impeachment, notes, outside research, deliberation, and the verdict form.

docs.t: Judge Helen W. Gillmor (D. Haw.) — Electronic devices (trap)
docs.x: Judge Helen W. Gillmor, D. Haw.. Electronic devices (trap): Under the November 6, 2008 General Order, attorneys of record may bring laptops, phones, and tablets into the courthouse only for use in case-related proceedings in the courtroom or chambers, and must tell court security at the entrance the time of their proceeding and the case name. The order does not cover paralegals, other staff, parties, or witnesses. The authorization does not apply when counsel enters for a matter other than a hearing or conference with Judge Gillmor. Cell phones must be off in the courtroom unless the court permits, and no camera or audio/video equipment may be used in hearings or chambers.

docs.t: Judge Helen W. Gillmor (D. Haw.) — Contact
docs.x: Judge Helen W. Gillmor, D. Haw.. Contact: Chambers (808) 541-3502; orders to gillmor_orders@hid.uscourts.gov. Courtroom manager Theresa Lam, (808) 541-3577, theresa_lam@hid.uscourts.gov.

docs.t: Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.) — Contacting chambers (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jill Otake, D. Haw.. Contacting chambers (trap): Request any action only by filing a letter or motion; do not email or call chambers. If urgent, email otake_orders@hid.uscourts.gov to say an urgent request has been filed. (In criminal cases, agreed sentencing reschedules are the exception.) Questions about practices: read the procedures and Local Rules first, then email otake_orders@hid.uscourts.gov copying all counsel and self-represented parties. Phone inquiries are disfavored. Failure to follow the procedures may draw sanctions.

docs.t: Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.) — Remote appearances
docs.x: Judge Jill Otake, D. Haw.. Remote appearances: File a letter request as soon as practicable and no later than 36 hours before the hearing. Telephonic appearances at dispositive motion hearings are disfavored. No recording by remote attendees.

docs.t: Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.) — Continuances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jill Otake, D. Haw.. Continuances (trap): Every motion-hearing continuance, even a joint one, requires a filed motion stating which number continuance it is (e.g., “First Motion to Continue …”), filed well ahead. Civil trial: a joint request more than 5 months before trial may go by stipulation to the magistrate judge showing good cause; within 5 months a motion is required. Continuances over 6 months are disfavored. State prior continuances and any deadlines to reopen or extend; proposed orders go to otake_orders@hid.uscourts.gov in Word, copying all parties. Criminal: the first trial continuance may be by stipulation and proposed order; later or opposed continuances need a motion and proposed order stating prior continuances and opposition. Confer with the courtroom manager for a new trial date first. An unopposed sentencing continuance may be requested by email to the courtroom

docs.t: Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.) — Motions and meet-and-confer (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jill Otake, D. Haw.. Motions and meet-and-confer (trap): Local Rule 7.8 conferences must be by lead counsel in real time; letters or emails do not count. Many motions to dismiss or strike could be avoided by conferring: plaintiff’s counsel must carefully evaluate claimed pleading defects, and in most instances the moving party should agree to any amendment that would cure a curable defect. Leave to exceed L.R. 7.4 page or word limits requires a motion and is granted only in limited circumstances; noncompliant briefs may be stricken. Cite Westlaw rather than Lexis unless unavailable. Review General Order 23-1 on unverified sources (AI); noncompliance may draw sanctions. Stipulations to dismiss go to otake_orders@hid.uscourts.gov in Word. Rule 41(a) does not permit dismissing fewer than all claims against a defendant; use Rule 15(a) (Hells Canyon).

docs.t: Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.) — Chambers copies and sealing
docs.x: Judge Jill Otake, D. Haw.. Chambers copies and sealing: One chambers copy of motions, oppositions, replies, and attachments. None needed for answers, notices of appearance, motions to exceed page limits, or motions to continue (criminal: also government appearance applications, trial continuance motions, and sentencing statements). Up to 50 pages may be stapled; longer documents go in labeled binders. Motions to seal are not considered until L.R. 5.2(c) (Crim. L.R. 5.2(b)) is fully met. Submit one courtesy copy plus the documents to be sealed immediately after filing, and email electronic copies to otake_orders@hid.uscourts.gov.

docs.t: Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jill Otake, D. Haw.. Summary judgment (trap): One motion only: no splitting summary judgment across multiple motions. Each concise-statement fact is one sentence with a citation, separately numbered. The Opposing Concise Statement is a 2-column chart repeating every moving fact with a response (undisputed, disputed and why, or disputed in part and why) and pincites. The movant’s Response is a 3-column chart (landscape allowed).

docs.t: Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.) — Daubert and motions in limine
docs.x: Judge Jill Otake, D. Haw.. Daubert and motions in limine: Daubert motions are non-dispositive and follow the scheduling order deadlines; Daubert issues may not be raised in motions in limine. File each motion in limine separately; memoranda and oppositions are limited to 5 pages. Avoid broad requests (e.g., to preclude all hearsay). Local Rule 7.8 compliance is required for civil motions in limine.

docs.t: Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.) — Trial schedule and jury selection
docs.x: Judge Jill Otake, D. Haw.. Trial schedule and jury selection: Trials start Mondays (unless a holiday). Jury trials run 8:30 a.m. to 2:30 or 3 p.m. (4:30 p.m. on selection days), with breaks around 10:30 a.m. (15 minutes) and noon (20 minutes). Matters outside the jury’s presence are heard at 8:15 a.m. and at the end of the day; raise them at the end of the day. Bench trials run 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. In civil cases the judge limits each party’s hours. Each side typically gets 10 minutes of voir dire (more on request). Challenges for cause must be made in the moment; peremptories are made on paper without jurors knowing. No attorney voir dire in cases with pro se parties.

docs.t: Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.) — Jury instructions and exhibits
docs.x: Judge Jill Otake, D. Haw.. Jury instructions and exhibits: Submissions derived from the judge’s standard instructions or model instructions must be redlined to show changes; jurors receive hard copies. Mark exhibits by number in tabbed 3-ring binders with labeled spines; coordinate numbering with the courtroom manager and do not designate by party (“Exhibit 1,” not “Plaintiff’s Exhibit 1”). Number each photograph separately, and number groups of documents separately unless the witness testifies to the group as a whole. Civil: provide original depositions in labeled manila folders, alphabetically.

docs.t: Judge Jill Otake (D. Haw.) — Criminal hearings and pleas
docs.x: Judge Jill Otake, D. Haw.. Criminal hearings and pleas: Evidentiary hearings (including sentencing): file exhibit and witness lists at least 2 business days before; exhibit binders to the courtroom manager 1 business day before. Schedule guilty pleas with the courtroom manager at least 5 calendar days ahead. Email plea agreements to otake_orders@hid.uscourts.gov at least 2 business days before the hearing; without an agreement, the government emails a memo then covering the charging document, penalties, elements, expected facts, and other useful information.

docs.t: Judge John Michael Seabright (D. Haw.) — Electronic devices: counsel (trap)
docs.x: Judge John Michael Seabright, D. Haw.. Electronic devices: counsel (trap): On request, the judge may permit an attorney of record, or staff such as a paralegal working for one, to use a computer, tablet, or smartphone in the courtroom for case-related matters. Permission is discretionary, so ask first. No device may disrupt proceedings, cell phones must always be silenced, and no device may be connected to the internet in the courtroom without the court’s permission. No photographing or audio/video recording of proceedings in the courtroom or chambers; violations draw sanctions.

docs.t: Judge John Michael Seabright (D. Haw.) — Electronic devices: everyone else
docs.x: Judge John Michael Seabright, D. Haw.. Electronic devices: everyone else: Everyone other than attorneys of record must turn devices completely off before entering the courtroom; no recording, photography, texting, internet searching, or calls. Violators may be removed, sanctioned, or have the device confiscated. The judge may modify these rules for specific cases or proceedings, including approving media blogging in advance.

docs.t: Judge John Michael Seabright (D. Haw.) — Civil jury instructions
docs.x: Judge John Michael Seabright, D. Haw.. Civil jury instructions: The judge posts preliminary instructions (duty of jury, evidence, objections, credibility, bench conferences, burden of proof, juror conduct including no AI or internet research, no transcript, notes, and trial outline) and final instructions (evidence, depositions, interrogatories, admissions, experts, impeachment, burden of proof, multiple parties, damages, notes, deliberation, and verdict form), with bracketed options to adapt. Word versions are posted for editing.

docs.t: Judge John Michael Seabright (D. Haw.) — Juror questions

docs.x: Judge Leslie E. Kobayashi, D. Haw.. Pretrial and settlement: Settlement conferences with the magistrate judge are set at the Rule 16 conference, and the judge may hold a further one. The judge holds a pretrial conference 2 weeks before trial; be ready to discuss witnesses and scheduling, settlement status, interpreter or AV needs, and exhibits and motions in limine. Motions in limine follow the scheduling order deadlines and are decided without hearing by the day before jury selection; ask at the final pretrial conference for an earlier hearing.

docs.t: Judge Leslie E. Kobayashi (D. Haw.) — Video access and electronic devices
docs.x: Judge Leslie E. Kobayashi, D. Haw.. Stay muted, do not record, and do not share login information. The amended device order lets attorneys of record bring devices only for proceedings before the judge, telling security the case and time; phones off. Any camera use can bring extremely severe sanctions, including a recommendation of suspension or disbarment, and a ringing phone can draw sanctions.

docs.t: Judge Leslie E. Kobayashi (D. Haw.) — Trial schedule and conduct
docs.x: Judge Leslie E. Kobayashi, D. Haw.. Sidebars are highly discouraged; counsel meet with the judge at 8:15 a.m., at recess, or after the jury leaves. Each side gets 10 to 15 minutes of voir dire after the court’s questioning. Stay at the podium and use the microphone. No demonstratives in opening without all parties’ stipulation. Disclose the next day’s witnesses by the close of each trial day. Motions during trial should generally be written.

After rulings, file and serve a declaration with the redacted Working Copy before publication; provide a reader if read aloud.

docs.t: Judge Micah W. J. Smith (D. Haw.) — Remote appearances
docs.x: Judge Micah W. J. Smith, D. Haw.. Remote appearances: File a letter request on ECF at least one week before the hearing, explaining why remote appearance is warranted. docs.t: Judge Micah W. J. Smith (D. Haw.) — Pre-filing conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge Micah W. J. Smith, D. Haw.. Pre-filing conference (trap): Local Rule 7.8 conferences must be conducted by lead counsel, by a method that puts all parties in real-time communication, and in enough detail that any motion addresses only the issues still requiring resolution. Letters and emails do not count as a proper conference.

docs.t: Judge Micah W. J. Smith (D. Haw.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Micah W. J. Smith, D. Haw.. Motions: Parties are strongly encouraged (not required) to state in the motion or opposition whether a hearing should be held (L.R. 7.1(c)). Requests to divide oral argument among counsel may be made by email, through the courtroom manager, or at the start of the hearing, and are likely to be granted. The judge encourages giving junior attorneys argument opportunities and will let experienced counsel step in as needed. In criminal cases, defense motions to withdraw are usually heard by the judge, not referred to a magistrate judge, and must be filed as early as possible to protect trial dates.

docs.t: Judge Micah W. J. Smith (D. Haw.) — Motions to dismiss and amendment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Micah W. J. Smith, D. Haw.. Motions to dismiss and amendment (trap): If a defendant moves to dismiss the initial complaint, the plaintiff may amend within 14 days of the motion without leave; the court then denies the motion as moot without prejudice. Within 14 days after service of the first amended complaint, the defendant must answer, file a new or supplemental motion to dismiss (which may incorporate the earlier briefing and exhibits by reference), or file an ECF letter relying on the earlier motion. If the defendant renews its motion, the plaintiff may not file a second amended complaint without leave.

docs.t: Judge Micah W. J. Smith (D. Haw.) — Daubert motions and motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Micah W. J. Smith, D. Haw.. Daubert motions and motions in limine (trap): Daubert motions are treated as non-dispositive and must meet the Rule 16 Scheduling Order deadlines; Daubert issues may not be raised in motions in limine. If a dispositive motion is intertwined with a Daubert motion, contact the courtroom manager to request a status conference on scheduling. Each motion in limine memorandum and opposition is limited to ten pages; seek leave for an overlength brief if a single issue needs more. There is no limit on the number of motions in limine, but each requires an adequate L.R. 7.8 conference.

docs.x: Judge Micah W. J. Smith, D. Haw.. Civil continuances (trap): Unopposed joint requests to continue a hearing may go through the courtroom manager or by email (copying all counsel); opposed requests require an ECF motion stating which number continuance is sought (for example, “Second Motion to Continue …”). Ask well in advance. If trial is more than five months away and all agree, submit a stipulation showing good cause to the assigned magistrate judge. If any party opposes, or trial is five months away or less, submit a stipulation or motion (with proposed order) to Judge Smith, stating the number of prior continuances and whether closed deadlines are to be reopened or current ones extended. Continuances pushing trial back more than six months are disfavored and must be justified with particularity.

docs.t: Judge Micah W. J. Smith (D. Haw.) — Criminal scheduling and continuances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Micah W. J. Smith, D. Haw.. Criminal scheduling and continuances (trap): Shortly after the initial appearance, the judge holds a status conference; the defendant and defense counsel must be ready to say whether they can be prepared for trial within the 70-day Speedy Trial default. If more time is needed, come prepared to propose how much; the court will set a motions deadline, exclude time, and usually set trial within 70 days after the motions deadline. Once the trial date is confirmed or set this way, motions to continue it are viewed with great disfavor, require a motion and proposed order, and will likely be set for hearing. Continuances based on reasons or conflicts known when the date was set are highly unlikely to be granted. Unopposed requests to continue criminal hearings (for example, sentencing) may go through the courtroom manager or by email; opposed requests require a

docs.t: Judge Micah W. J. Smith (D. Haw.) — Settlement (trap)
docs.x: Judge Micah W. J. Smith, D. Haw.. Settlement (trap): The judge will not retain jurisdiction to enforce a confidential settlement. To have the court retain jurisdiction, the parties must put the settlement terms on the public record and request retention before dismissal, even if a magistrate judge took the settlement.

docs.t: Judge Micah W. J. Smith (D. Haw.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Micah W. J. Smith, D. Haw.. Trial: Jury trials usually start on Mondays and run Monday to Friday, 9:00 a.m. to 3:45 p.m., with breaks at about 10:30 a.m. (10 minutes), 12:00 to 12:45 p.m., and 2:30 p.m. (10 minutes). Counsel must appear at 8:45 a.m. daily and be ready to stay after 3:45 p.m.; to appear earlier, email the courtroom manager early on the preceding trial day. Bench trials generally follow the same schedule, but the judge will confer on a case-specific schedule, including unusually long or short days. To tailor a trial schedule, email the courtroom manager (copying all counsel) to request a pretrial conference. Criminal trials: the court conducts all voir dire from questions the parties submit; counsel may not question jurors directly. Civil trials: each side gets up to 20 minutes of its own voir dire, but the court conducts most of it, so submit proposed questions.

docs.t: Judge Micah W. J. Smith (D. Haw.) — Courtroom conduct and feedback
docs.x: Judge Micah W. J. Smith, D. Haw.. Courtroom conduct and feedback: Inside the courtroom only attorneys of record and their litigation team may use electronic devices, and only for the ongoing case-related proceeding; ask if in doubt. No cameras or recording equipment in the courtroom or chambers; violations draw sanctions. Parties must act with the highest professionalism, including in discovery and depositions. After a case is finally resolved, counsel may request a feedback meeting in chambers by email to smith_orders@hid.uscourts.gov; all counsel of record must participate or consent.

docs.x: Judge Shanlyn A. S. Park, D. Haw.. docs.t: Judge Shanlyn A. S. Park (D. Haw.) — Remote appearances

docs.x: Judge Shanlyn A. S. Park, D. Haw.. Chambers copies and proposed orders: No more than one chambers copy of motions and attachments. Continuances of more than 6 months are disfavored and need particularized reasons. Criminal: a Rule 17.1 pretrial conference follows the initial appearance; be ready to discuss discovery, motions, and trial readiness, and any requested continuance length. Later tr

docs.t: Judge Shanlyn A. S. Park (D. Haw.) — Trial schedule and voir dire
docs.x: Judge Shanlyn A. S. Park, D. Haw.. Trial schedule and voir dire: Jury trials start Tuesdays and run 9 a.m. to 2:30 or 3 p.m. (to 4:30 p.m. on jury selection days), with breaks at about 11 a.m. (15 minutes) and 12:30 p.m. (20 minutes). Bench trials run 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. with lunch from noon to 1:30 p.m. The court conducts general voir dire, incorporating parties’ special questions; each side then has 20 minutes (more may be considered in complex cases).

docs.t: Judge Shanlyn A. S. Park (D. Haw.) — Trial conduct and exhibits
docs.x: Judge Shanlyn A. S. Park, D. Haw.. Trial conduct and exhibits: Sidebars are highly discouraged; defer disputes to recess. Speak at the podium using the microphone, state only the basis of objections, and make offers of proof outside the jury’s presence. Disclose the next day’s witnesses by the close of each trial day; the exclusionary rule applies from motions/jury selection through closings. No demonstratives shown to the jury without permission or stipulation. Agree on a common exhibit set and report agreed and disputed exhibits (by number) by the motions in limine hearing. Provide one set of exhibits in separate labeled manila folders, one tabbed binder set, and JERS electronic exhibits on the same day. Exhibits are generally not passed among jurors. Motions during trial should generally be written; special equipment needs advance permission.

docs.x: Judge Shanlyn A. S. Park, D. Haw.. Jury instructions and bench trials: Instructions derived from Ninth Circuit or other model instructions must be redlined to show changes. Civil bench trials: trial briefs by the Scheduling Order deadline; after ruling, the prevailing party drafts findings of fact and conclusions of law annotated to the transcript, and the other side files objections and revisions.

docs.x: Judge Andrew B. Davis, W.D. Tex.. Joint discovery and case management plan: The judge’s Joint Discovery and Case Management Plan form asks for jurisdiction details (for LLCs, LLPs, and partnerships, every member’s citizenship, plus an attached affidavit or declaration), removal service dates, the elements of each claim and defense with supporting authority, related cases, unserved parties, and discovery, settlement, ADR, and consent positions. Parties may agree to extend discovery deadlines with written notice if later deadlines are unaffected, but the court can reject the extension. Non-discovery deadlines and continuances will not be extended, even on joint motion, without actual diligence and extraordinary cause. Rebuttal experts are due 30 days after the disclosure being rebutted. Attorney’s-fees experts are exempt; fees are sought by Rule 54(d)(2) motion after judgment.

If no dispositive motion is filed, the parties must jointly file a notice saying so, so trial can be set.

A joint report signed by all counsel (date, attendees and capacities, whether meaningful progress was made, and prospects) is due within 7 days.

docs.t: Judge Andrew B. Davis (W.D. Tex.) — Referrals to the magistrate judge

docs.x: Judge David Briones, W.D. Tex.. docs.x: Judge David Briones, W.D. Tex.. docs.x: Judge David Briones, W.D. Tex.. Motions and briefing: No courtesy copies, and no copies of cases attached to briefs. If the parties are amenable to ADR, tell the court and it will order it. The court generally appoints the mediator but will consider a recommendation with a supporting explanation. docs.x: Judge David Briones, W.D. Tex.. Civil trial: No docket calls. Address the court from the lectern. Trial hours, decorum, jury questionnaires, opening time, and deposition excerpts are covered in the law clerk’s letter sent after the scheduling order. docs.x: Judge David Briones, W.D. Tex.. Criminal cases (trap): Scheduling is governed by the court’s Standing Discovery Order (not posted); changes require a motion. Pleas are referred to the magistrate judge. Counsel must confer on all motions before filing (unless an ex parte communication is justified) and state the result in the motion. The court prefers pretrial motion practice over the pretrial checklist; coordinate motions to suppress and evidentiary sentencing hearings with the courtroom deputy. Make a good-faith attempt to resolve discovery disputes before seeking court intervention. Communicate PSR objections to the probation officer rather than filing them. Attorney-conducted voir dire is allowed if the court finds it appropriate; opening time depends on the case. The court frowns on one attorney representing multiple defendants in one case.

docs.x: Judge David Briones, W.D. Tex.. Sanctions and pet peeves: The most common grounds for sanctions are discovery abuse and failing to appear for scheduled hearings. The court will not tolerate tardiness or unpreparedness.

docs.t: Judge David C. Guaderrama (W.D. Tex.) — Bill of costs (trap)
docs.x: Judge David C. Guaderrama, W.D. Tex.. Bill of costs (trap): Before moving for costs, review the law summarized in the order, send the proposed bill to opposing counsel, and meet, confer, and try to submit an agreed bill. If a legitimate dispute remains, file a motion under Rule 54 and Local Rule CV-54 identifying the disagreements; the court will set a hearing at which lead trial counsel must appear and explain why they could not resolve it. The order notes, among other things, that private process server fees, postage, faxes, electronic legal research, travel, meals, and mediation fees generally are not recoverable, document translation is not interpreter compensation, and video and transcript versions of a deposition each require a showing of necessity.

docs.t: Judge David C. Guaderrama (W.D. Tex.) — Immigration habeas cases
docs.x: Judge David C. Guaderrama, W.D. Tex.. If the other side disagrees with how the facts are characterized, it must tell the court within 3 days. The order is docketed in all pending and future “463 Habeas Corpus – Alien Detainee” cases assigned to the judge.

docs.x: Judge David C. Guaderrama, W.D. Tex.. Social Security referrals: Social Security appeals assigned to the judge are referred to an El Paso magistrate judge for nondispositive pretrial matters and findings and recommendations on dispositive motions.

docs.t: Judge Kathleen Cardone (W.D. Tex.) — Hearings and contact
docs.x: Judge Kathleen Cardone, W.D. Tex.. Hearings and contact: The court ordinarily does not hold hearings on civil motions; to ask for one, say so with reasons in the opening paragraph of the motion or response. No telephone conferences to resolve motions. Do not call about the status of civil motions or about substantive issues. Procedural questions not answered by the rules or standing orders may go to the law clerks at (915) 534-6740. Notify a law clerk immediately when a pending motion is resolved, and notify the court immediately when a motion is unopposed or the case settles. No chambers copies are required. For a TRO, after filing and assignment notify a law clerk or the courtroom deputy, try to give the other side notice, and send it a copy by fax or email.

docs.t: Judge Kathleen Cardone (W.D. Tex.) — Civil motion format (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kathleen Cardone, W.D. Tex.. Civil motion format (trap): Every civil motion, opposition, and reply must contain: only the title below the caption on page 1; a statement of issues of no more than 1 page; a succinct statement of facts; argument with authority; and, if over 10 pages, a table of contents and table of authorities. The title page, tables, and statement of issues do not count toward the CV-7 page limit. Noncompliant filings will not be accepted. Longer briefs need leave (routinely granted); additional briefing beyond the reply needs leave; no letter briefs. Do not combine a motion to dismiss with an answer, or a response with a motion, in one document. Hyperlinking citations to Westlaw or Lexis is encouraged.

docs.t: Judge Kathleen Cardone (W.D. Tex.) — Pretrial deadlines (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kathleen Cardone, W.D. Tex.. A motion to dismiss does not stay discovery. Changes need a particularized showing of good cause, and extending one deadline does not extend later ones. Requests to modify the scheduling order must be by motion; any request to move the trial date must be made in writing before the discovery deadline.

docs.t: Judge Kathleen Cardone (W.D. Tex.) — Summary judgment

The opposition’s “Response to Proposed Undisputed Facts” admits or denies each paragraph and lists “Disputed Issues of Material Fact” in a separate section. Each fact and denial needs a specific citation to competent affidavits or admissible evidence, filed with the statements; failing to cite can lead to denial or grant of the motion. Movants against a pro se party must serve the order’s form notice with Rule 56 and the order attached.
