docs.x: Judge Ana C. Reyes, D.D.C.. Briefing format (trap): Double-spaced, 12-point Times New Roman, 1-inch margins, page numbers, and two spaces between sentences; every citation needs a pin cite. Noncompliant motions may be rejected. Absent leave, opening and opposition memoranda may not exceed 45 pages and replies 25. Any memorandum of 10 pages or more needs a table of contents and table of authorities. Filings must be text-searchable PDFs, with each attachment (memorandum, statement of facts, exhibit, affidavit, proposed order) filed as a separate, labeled PDF and an exhibit index when there is more than one exhibit. Sur-replies only with leave on a specific showing of good cause, and the motion for leave must not attach the proposed sur-reply. Supplemental authorities need no leave but must be filed as a pleading (not a letter) following FRAP 28(j), without reargument. Every amended pleadin

docs.x: Judge Ana C. Reyes, D.D.C.. Courtesy copies and proposed orders (trap): Civil: for any filing that with exhibits totals 50 pages or more, the movant delivers two printed copies with ECF headers to chambers (not the Clerk’s Office), but only once briefing is complete, including oppositions, replies, sur-replies, and, for dispositive motions, the operative complaint. Pro se, IFP, and incarcerated plaintiffs are excused. The movant also provides one jointly prepared, tabbed, alphabetical, single-sided three-ring binder of key cases. A proposed order is required with any req

docs.t: Judge Ana C. Reyes (D.D.C.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Ana C. Reyes, D.D.C.. Summary judgment (trap): Local Civil Rule 7(h) is strictly enforced. The movant’s Statement of Material Facts Not in Dispute is a two-column table with one undisputed fact per numbered row in the left column, with record cites, and the movant must promptly send an editable copy to the opponent. The opponent files a Counter-Statement of Disputed Facts answering each row in the right column (admitted or denied, with cites, specifying partial admissions), then adds its additional facts and its list of genuinely disputed material facts in consecutively numbered rows at the end, and sends an editable copy back. The movant files a Reply to Counter-Statement responding to the additional facts in the left column. Noncompliance may lead to denial without prejudice or to facts being treated as undisputed.

docs.t: Judge Ana C. Reyes (D.D.C.) — Meet and confer, extensions, and contact (trap)
docs.x: Judge Ana C. Reyes, D.D.C.. Meet and confer, extensions, and contact (trap): LCvR 7(m) is strictly enforced: an adequate certificate almost always requires at least two personal communications, and unanswered emails are not enough. Noncompliant non-dispositive motions will be stricken. Extensions only by motion, never by stipulation, filed at least 4 days before the deadline (4 business days in criminal cases) and stating the original date, prior extensions, good cause, effect on other deadlines, proposed briefing dates or three alternative hearing dates, and the opponent’s position. Opposition reasons are due by 5:00 p.m. the next (business) day or the motion is deemed conceded. Late motions need an explanation and are denied absent compelling cause. No telephone calls to chambers except as the orders allow; in emergencies, call jointly. For after-hours emergency motions, notify chamber

docs.t: Judge Ana C. Reyes (D.D.C.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Ana C. Reyes, D.D.C.. Discovery disputes: After good-faith conferral, send a short joint email to Reyes_Chambers@dcd.uscourts.gov requesting a teleconference, with a concise description of the issues, each side’s positions with citations, and responses to opposing arguments. Leave of court is required before filing any discovery motion; otherwise it may be stricken.

docs.t: Judge Ana C. Reyes (D.D.C.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Ana C. Reyes, D.D.C.. Sealing: File a public redacted version with the motion to seal, or state specifically why the whole document must stay sealed. A protective-order designation alone is not enough. Confer with the opposing party first and include the conferral results and a Hubbard-factor analysis in the motion (civil and criminal).

docs.t: Judge Ana C. Reyes (D.D.C.) — Scheduling, appearances, and oral argument
docs.x: Judge Ana C. Reyes, D.D.C.. Scheduling, appearances, and oral argument: After an answer, the court sets an initial scheduling conference; the joint LCvR 16.3 report must propose three alternative trial dates. The trial date will not move absent extraordinary cause, “the legal equivalent of Armageddon.” Principal trial counsel must attend all conferences absent leave, every appearing attorney must file a notice of appearance and have authority to bind the client, and all parties or party representatives must attend the pretrial conference. Request oral argument in the motion papers. Argument is more likely if a junior attorney will get courtroom experience. Removed or transferred cases: refile pending motions (within 7 days after a transfer order is docketed) or they are deemed withdrawn; a removing defendant must refile its answer and serve this order; an unanswered transferred complaint

docs.t: Judge Ana C. Reyes (D.D.C.) — Civil pretrial and trial
docs.x: Judge Ana C. Reyes, D.D.C.. Civil pretrial and trial: Joint Pretrial Statement at least 14 days before the final pretrial conference, with the LCvR 16.5 contents, a six-column exhibit list, and an eight-column deposition-objection chart in transcript page order (with blank “Sustained” and “Overruled” columns). Jury cases add agreed and disputed voir dire, joint jury instructions with redlined objections and sources, and a verdict form. Motions in limine must be fully briefed when the pretrial statement is filed: motion at least 21 days before it is due, opposition in 14 days, reply in 7. No omnibus motions; file one numbered motion per issue. In bench trials, proposed findings and conclusions are due within one week after the close of evidence. To mediate, move for referral to a magistrate judge or the court’s mediation program; plaintiff must promptly file notice of any settlement.

docs.x: Judge Ana C. Reyes, D.D.C.. Plea materials (agreement or outline and Rule 11(c) type, reasons for any out-of-guidelines sentence, elements, factual proffer, penalties, guideline estimate, and immigration notice for noncitizens) go to the deputy and chambers at least 5 business days before the hearing. docs.x: Judge Carl J. Nichols, D.D.C.. Contact with chambers (trap): No telephone calls to chambers except to report an actual emergency. Scheduling inquiries go to the courtroom deputy, Courtney Moore (Courtney_Moore@dcd.uscourts.gov, 202-354-3101). Chambers gives no legal advice.

docs.x: Judge Carl J. Nichols, D.D.C.. docs.t: Judge Carl J. Nichols (D.D.C.) — Briefing format
docs.x: Judge Carl J. Nichols, D.D.C.. Briefing format: Memoranda of 10 pages or more need a table of contents and table of authorities. Every page is numbered at the bottom. One-inch margins; body double-spaced in 12-point Times New Roman; footnotes single-spaced, 12-point Times New Roman, with 12-point spacing between them. Page limits follow LCvR 7(e). Avoid excessive footnotes and acronyms, and define uncommon acronyms on first use; if the acronym limit makes the page limit unworkable, move for excess pages. Submissions with more than one exhibit need an exhibit index, and exhibits should be edited to the pertinent portions.

docs.t: Judge Carl J. Nichols (D.D.C.) — Extensions of time (trap)
docs.x: Judge Carl J. Nichols, D.D.C.. Extensions of time (trap): Discouraged. Granted only on motion, never by stipulation, and the motion should be filed at least 4 days before the deadline (or explain why not). The motion must state the original deadline, the number of prior extensions for each party, good cause, the effect on other deadlines, proposed opposition and reply dates agreed with the other side (for motion deadlines), and the opposing party’s position with reasons (LCvR 7(m)). Any opposition to an extension motion is due by 5:00 PM the business day after the motion is filed.

docs.t: Judge Carl J. Nichols (D.D.C.) — Rescheduling hearings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Carl J. Nichols, D.D.C.. Rescheduling hearings (trap): Discouraged. Meet and confer, then file a motion at least 1 week before the hearing (or explain why not) showing good cause and proposing four alternative dates and times convenient for all parties; if none work, the court picks. Weather or emergency closures are rescheduled by the courtroom deputy.

docs.t: Judge Carl J. Nichols (D.D.C.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Carl J. Nichols, D.D.C.. Summary judgment (trap): LCvR 7(h) is strictly enforced: facts in the movant’s statement are assumed admitted unless controverted in the opposing statement. Movant’s statement: numbered paragraphs, one factual assertion each. The response answers each paragraph in a matching numbered paragraph, admitting or denying (identifying admitted and denied parts) with specific record citations. Additional facts go in consecutively numbered paragraphs at the end of the response, and the movant must then file its own responsive statement.

docs.t: Judge Carl J. Nichols (D.D.C.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Carl J. Nichols, D.D.C.. Discovery disputes (trap): Confer in good faith first. If unresolved, arrange a telephone conference through the courtroom deputy and, beforehand, jointly email a short summary of the dispute to Nichols_Chambers@dcd.uscourts.gov. No discovery motion without leave.

docs.t: Judge Carl J. Nichols (D.D.C.) — Pleadings, removal, and scheduling
docs.x: Judge Carl J. Nichols, D.D.C.. Pleadings, removal, and scheduling: Plaintiff must serve the complaint promptly, file proof of service (LCvR 5.3), and serve the standing order on all parties. A removing defendant must refile the original complaint and any answer as a supplement to the notice of removal, serve the standing order, and refile any pending motion (Rule 81(c)(2)). Amended pleadings must include a redline against the original. After the answer, the court orders a Joint Meet and Confer Report covering all LCvR 16.3(c) topics, holds an initial scheduling conference if needed, and then issues a scheduling order.

docs.t: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan (D.D.C.) — Contact with chambers (trap)
docs.x: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, D.D.C.. Contact with chambers (trap): No ex parte communication with the judge or law clerks, and no ex parte phone calls. Communicate only by motion, opposition, and reply, not letter or phone, including for status, scheduling, or clarification of orders. In an actual emergency, call chambers only with all counsel and pro se parties on the line; otherwise contact the courtroom deputy, Mark Coates (202-354-3364). No faxes or emails to chambers unless the court asks. CM/ECF questions go to the help line (202-354-3190).

docs.t: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan (D.D.C.) — Motion format
docs.x: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, D.D.C.. Motion format: All submissions double-spaced, 12-point Times New Roman, one-inch margins. Memoranda of 10 pages or longer, supporting or opposing, need a table of contents and table of authorities. Any submission with more than one exhibit needs an exhibit index.

docs.t: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan (D.D.C.) — Extensions and continuances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, D.D.C.. Extensions and continuances (trap): Extensions only on motion, never by stipulation. Absent extenuating circumstances, file at least 3 business days before the hearing or deadline, with alternative dates agreed by all parties; requests without one may be denied.

docs.t: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan (D.D.C.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, D.D.C.. Summary judgment (trap): For motions not based solely on an administrative record, the movant files a separate Statement of Material Facts Not in Dispute as a two-column table: one fact per numbered row in the left column, with record citations. Promptly send the other side an editable electronic copy. The opponent files a Counter-Statement of Disputed Facts, admitting or denying each fact in the right column with record citations (specifying any partial admission), adding new facts in numbered rows at the end, and then listing the facts it says are genuinely disputed for trial; it too sends an editable copy. The movant then files a Reply to Counter-Statement responding to the additional facts in the left column. Noncompliance can mean denial without prejudice or facts deemed undisputed. A Material Facts Template shows the format.

docs.t: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan (D.D.C.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, D.D.C.. Discovery disputes (trap): Confer in good faith first. No discovery motion without leave of court; disputes may be referred to a magistrate judge.

docs.t: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan (D.D.C.) — Motions to dismiss and amendments
docs.x: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, D.D.C.. Motions to dismiss and amendments: Plaintiffs are directed to weigh a motion to dismiss carefully and fix defects by amending as of right under Rule 15(a) (within 21 days of service). A motion relying on matters outside the pleadings may be converted to summary judgment, and the summary judgment format then applies. Any amended submission must include a redline against the original.

docs.t: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan (D.D.C.) — Meet and confer report
docs.x: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, D.D.C.. Meet and confer report: Unless ordered otherwise, the LCvR 16.3 report and proposed scheduling order are due 30 days after any defendant answers or 14 days after a Rule 12(b) motion is decided. Include a brief statement of the case and consider the full range of ADR options. Cases exempt from LCvR 16.3 get a separate order.

docs.t: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan (D.D.C.) — Service, removal, and settlement
docs.x: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, D.D.C.. Service, removal, and settlement: If the standing order is docketed before defendants appear, plaintiffs (other than IFP plaintiffs) must serve it with or promptly after the complaint. A removing defendant must refile any answer as a supplement to the petition, serve the standing order, and refile any pending motion (Rule 81(c)(2)). Promptly notify the court of any full or partial settlement; without a stipulation of dismissal, the court may dismiss subject to reconsideration by a date certain.

docs.t: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan (D.D.C.) — Criminal cases: Brady order (trap)
docs.x: Judge Emmet G. Sullivan, D.D.C.. Criminal cases: Brady order (trap): The government must produce, timely and continuingly, all information favorable to the defense or in mitigation, including during plea negotiations and after conviction; doubts are resolved in favor of disclosure, and the Jencks Act or Rule 16 timing does not delay it. Production must be in readily usable form (as kept or clearly labeled; ESI as ordinarily maintained), in the original tangible format where one exists, or in a sufficiently detailed summary. Favorable information the government wants to withhold must be submitted for in camera review.

docs.t: Judge Randolph Moss (D.D.C.) — Summary judgment pre-motion conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge Randolph Moss, D.D.C.. Summary judgment pre-motion conference (trap): Before moving for summary judgment, request a pre-motion conference by filing on ECF a notice of no more than six double-spaced pages stating the basis for the motion, legal standards, and claims at issue; other parties respond within one week in a similar document. Not required of incarcerated pro se litigants. FOIA: the agency gives search declarations and any Vaughn index to the requester before seeking the conference. Motions to dismiss relying on matters outside the pleadings must follow the summary judgment instructions.

docs.t: Judge Randolph Moss (D.D.C.) — Summary judgment statements
docs.x: Judge Randolph Moss, D.D.C.. Summary judgment statements: LCvR 7(h) is strictly followed: one factual assertion per numbered paragraph, each with a precise record citation. Responses match each paragraph, admit or deny it (specifying partial admissions), and put additional facts in consecutively numbered paragraphs at the end; the movant must then respond to them. Uncontroverted facts may be deemed admitted. Agency-review cases: statements of facts cite the administrative record precisely (LCvR 7(h)(2)), and the parties file a joint appendix of cited record portions (LCvR 7(n)); if it exceeds 100 pages, deliver two printed courtesy copies.

docs.t: Judge Randolph Moss (D.D.C.) — Citation format (trap)
docs.x: Judge Randolph Moss, D.D.C.. Citation format (trap): Cite record material by PDF page number, not internal pagination: ECF page numbers for prior filings (e.g., Dkt. 50 at 5) and PDF pages for new exhibits, each filed separately (e.g., Ex. B at 5), with sections or paragraphs in a parenthetical (e.g., Dkt. 1 at 2 (Compl. ¶ 25)). File the entire exhibit relied on absent leave. Cite the U.S. Code, not only a separately enumerated statute section. Cite Westlaw, not Lexis, where possible. In pro se cases, give the pro se party copies of unpublished or database-only authorities.

docs.t: Judge Randolph Moss (D.D.C.) — Courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Randolph Moss, D.D.C.. Copies keep CM/ECF headers, in three-hole-punched binders, double-sided, tabbed, and indexed. Mail to chambers, not the Clerk’s Office; hand deliveries go to the loading dock. Copies are unredacted with publicly redacted portions highlighted. Pro se parties are excused.

docs.t: Judge Randolph Moss (D.D.C.) — Motions practice
docs.x: Judge Randolph Moss, D.D.C.. Motions practice: Memoranda of 10 pages or more, supporting or opposing, need a table of contents and table of authorities. Signature blocks include name, address, phone, and bar number, and note pro hac vice status. Noncompliant motions may be rejected. No sur-reply without leave on a specific showing of good cause. Supplemental authorities may be filed without leave, as a pleading rather than a letter, following FRAP 28(j), and must not reargue. Reconsideration motions are strongly discouraged and will not be entertained if they repeat rejected arguments or raise arguments that should have been made originally.

docs.x: Judge Randolph Moss, D.D.C.. docs.x: Judge Reggie Walton, D.D.C.. Sanctions for an incomplete report (trap): Failure to file a complete joint Report may lead to sanctions. docs.x: Judge Reggie Walton, D.D.C.. Phased discovery: For good cause, the parties may ask at the conference for discovery in phases to achieve proportionality, with a status conference after each phase.

docs.x: Judge Reggie Walton, D.D.C.. Civility: All counsel and parties must treat each other and everyone involved in the case, including witnesses, with dignity, respect, and civility, in and out of court.

docs.x: Judge Timothy J. Kelly, D.D.C.. The motion states the original deadline, time requested, prior extensions for each party, good cause, effect on other deadlines, a proposed schedule for affected deadlines after consulting opposing counsel, and the opponent’s position under LCvR 7(m). Any opposition is due by 5:00 p.m. the next business day. Rescheduling hearings is discouraged: meet and confer, then move at least one week before the hearing (or explain why not), showing good cause and proposing four alternative dates and times convenient for all parties. Weather or emergency closures are rescheduled by the courtroom deputy.

A protective order alone does not justify sealing. With proposed redactions, also file an unredacted copy with the proposed redactions highlighted.

docs.x: Judge Eric F. Melgren, D. Kan.. docs.t: Judge Eric F. Melgren (D. Kan.) — Sealing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Eric F. Melgren, D. Kan.. Sealing (trap): Documents are not automatically sealed because they were produced under a protective order or because the parties stipulate. Before attaching protected documents, first ask the opposing party whether a redaction agreement can avoid sealing. Otherwise, file a motion for leave to file under seal with the proposed sealed documents attached. Both the motion and the response (often the non-movant claims confidentiality) must show good cause with specific facts of public or private harm, not conclusory statements (citing JetAway Aviation and Helm v. Kansas). The court may rule on the papers or set a telephonic hearing. File under seal only after leave is granted; if denied, the court may permit filing not under seal.

docs.t: Judge Julie A. Robinson (D. Kan.) — Jury selection and time limits
docs.x: Judge Julie A. Robinson, D. Kan.. Jury selection and time limits: Struck method. Civil: 14 in the box, 3 peremptories per side, usually a jury of 8. Criminal: 32 in the box, 6 peremptories for the government and 10 total for defendants, plus 1 each for alternates; usually 12 jurors and 2 alternates. Peremptories are exercised in writing, alternating, starting with plaintiff or the government. The juror list (name, town, occupation) is available one week before trial. In civil cases, submit a joint statement of the case, generally no more than one page, for the court to read in voir dire. The court conducts extensive voir dire; each party gets 30 total minutes of supplemental questioning and may not argue or indoctrinate. Openings are usually limited to 20 minutes per party and closings to 30 minutes.

docs.t: Judge Julie A. Robinson (D. Kan.) — Trial day and witnesses (trap)
docs.x: Judge Julie A. Robinson, D. Kan.. Trial day and witnesses (trap): Trial hours vary: 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., 8:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. with no lunch break, or a combination. Matters outside the jury’s presence go at 8:30 a.m., at breaks, or after the trial day, with advance notice; bench conferences are kept to a minimum. Disclose the next day’s witnesses and exhibits to opposing counsel by 6:00 p.m. the day before. Have enough witnesses for a full day; there should be no dead time. Objections: “objection” plus the basis only (e.g., “hearsay”), no narrative. Give the court reporter your business card and, for technical terms, a glossary before trial.

docs.t: Judge Julie A. Robinson (D. Kan.) — Courtroom conduct
docs.x: Judge Julie A. Robinson, D. Kan.. Courtroom conduct: Stand when addressing the court and when the jury or the court enters or exits. Ask permission to approach the bench (no permission needed to approach a witness). Only one attorney per party examines a witness (Local Rule 43.1(b)), from the lectern, without greeting witnesses or using first names. No commenting on rulings, testimony, or opposing counsel, and no arguing after a ruling. No food, soft drinks, cups with logos, or straws; no boxes or briefcases on counsel tables. If the rule on witnesses is invoked, counsel must instruct their witnesses on the four listed sequestration limits. Avoid any contact with jurors; post-trial juror interviews require a court order (D. Kan. Rule 47.1).

docs.t: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil (D. Kan.) — Trial day and witness disclosure (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil, D. Kan.. Trial day and witness disclosure (trap): The goal is at least 7 hours of uninterrupted testimony every trial day, with legal issues heard outside the jury’s time rather than at bench conferences. Witnesses and exhibits expected to be used must be disclosed to opposing counsel 24 hours in advance, so issues can be raised the next day before the jury is seated or during a recess. On the first day of trial counsel must be present at 8:30 a.m. to go over procedures with the courtroom deputy or law clerk.

docs.t: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil (D. Kan.) — Exhibits and JERS (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil, D. Kan.. Exhibits and JERS (trap): For jury trials, original exhibits must be offered in electronic format to the extent possible, for use in JERS (not used in bench trials). The court’s standard JERS instructions require the exhibit device no later than 1 week before trial, files named “-_” (part in letters only), and defense exhibits starting at 801. At the outset of any hearing or trial, give the court a marked paper copy of exhibits in a 3-ring binder, and tell the courtroom deputy about stipulated exhibits so they can be received at the start. A second paper copy for the witness stand is recommended if you display exhibits electronically. Counsel maintain the official exhibit list, keep a record of exhibits admitted each day, and must review admitted exhibits with the courtroom deputy or law clerk at the end of each trial day.

docs.t: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil (D. Kan.) — Civil jury selection (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil, D. Kan.. Civil jury selection (trap): The court seats 8 to 10 jurors in a civil jury trial; each side has 3 peremptory challenges. The court conducts initial voir dire on standard subjects (biography, knowledge of the case, counsel, or witnesses, prior jury service and litigation, experience with the subject matter, hardship), so counsel need not propose questions on them. Each party then gets 20 minutes of supplemental questioning. In voir dire counsel may not argue, seek promises, ask about the law, jury instructions, or opinions on hypothetical facts, or otherwise try to ingratiate or indoctrinate the jury.

docs.t: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil (D. Kan.) — Openings, closings, and jurors
docs.x: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil, D. Kan.. Openings, closings, and jurors: Absent prior leave, each party gets 20 minutes for opening statement and 20 minutes for closing argument. Jurors may take notes, and the court may allow juror questions, screened before being asked in open court.

docs.x: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil, D. Kan.. Courtroom etiquette: Stand when court opens, recesses, and adjourns, when the jury enters or leaves, and when addressing or addressed by the court (counsel with physical disabilities excused). Refer to everyone, including witnesses, by surname with Mr., Ms., or another title, never by first name or nickname.

docs.t: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil (D. Kan.) — Criminal: Speedy Trial continuances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil, D. Kan.. Criminal: Speedy Trial continuances (trap): Under Pretrial Order No. 1, a motion to extend the 70-day trial deadline and exclude time under 18 U.S.C. § 3161(h)(7) must be filed jointly by the deadline set (at least 7 days before the status conference), with any disagreement set out in the joint motion. Later extension motions are closely scrutinized. Conclusory or boilerplate motions tracking the statute are insufficient (citing United States v. Toombs). The motion must address the listed factors (why the event requires time, complexity, diligence, other trials, witness unavailability, the defendant’s position, multi-defendant dates) and propose a firm schedule for discovery, motions, hearings, and trial days. Press of other business is ordinarily not enough; such a motion must address whether other counsel in the office could try the case. Counsel must

docs.t: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil (D. Kan.) — Criminal discovery
docs.x: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil, D. Kan.. Criminal discovery: Pretrial Order No. 1 makes discovery obligations self-executing; no request is needed, and boilerplate discovery motions are discouraged. The government’s Rule 16 disclosures are due at least 14 days before the pretrial-motion deadline, and the defendant’s reciprocal, alibi, and insanity disclosures within 14 days after. Brady material and Rule 404(b) notice (stating the specific purpose) are due no later than 14 days before trial; Giglio material sufficiently in advance for effective use. The court strongly urges Jencks statements at least 48 hours before the witness testifies. Expert summaries are due only on written request. Additional discovery requires a motion with memorandum and authority. Deadlines run from the original arraignment and do not restart on superseding charges; request a status conference if changes are needed.

docs.t: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil (D. Kan.) — Criminal pretrial and trial
docs.x: Judge Kathryn H. Vratil, D. Kan.. Criminal pretrial and trial: Under Pretrial Order No. 2, at least 14 days before the final pretrial conference counsel must finish conferring to narrow issues and file stipulations of fact and law, final witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine; responses are due at least 7 days before the conference, where motions in limine are argued. Trial settings are firm; continuances only for truly extraordinary circumstances. Tell the courtroom deputy immediately of a plea change or if fewer trial days are needed. Special voir dire requests and proposed jury instructions are due at least 7 days before trial; do not propose routine, standard instructions.

Facts not contradicted are deemed undisputed. Send a hard copy of voluminous record material with the filing. Noncompliant motions may be stricken or denied without notice. docs.t: Judge Alan Bond Johnson (D. Wyo.) — Contact, emergencies, and continuances
docs.x: Judge Alan Bond Johnson, D. Wyo.. Contact, emergencies, and continuances: Status inquiries go in writing to chambers (or, if absolutely necessary, to the judicial assistant at (307) 433-2170 or the courtroom deputy at (307) 433-2120), never to law clerks; no casual phone inquiries and no substantive arguments by letter. No faxes without permission. TRO and emergency applications are filed in CM/ECF with an affirmation that the other side was contacted and both can attend an in-chambers conference (or why contact isn’t required); ex parte TROs require compliance with Rule 65(b). Extension motions are not emergencies. Joint motions or agreements to continue do not bind the court. A trial generally will not be continued for an unavailable witness; plan to use a deposition or stipulation.

docs.t: Judge Alan Bond Johnson (D. Wyo.) — Appearances
docs.x: Judge Alan Bond Johnson, D. Wyo.. Appearances: Anyone appearing must know the case, have authority to bind the client, and be in charge. Telephone appearance needs chambers’ permission as early as possible; the requesting party sets up the call on a single line to (307) 433-2170 (landline preferred). Phone appearances are disfavored for evidentiary hearings. Notify chambers immediately when a matter set for hearing or trial settles; closing papers are due within 30 days.

docs.t: Judge Alan Bond Johnson (D. Wyo.) — Scheduling and criminal motions
docs.x: Judge Alan Bond Johnson, D. Wyo.. Scheduling and criminal motions: The joint Rule 26(f) report and proposed discovery/case management plan (Appendix A form, restating each bold instruction) is due at least 7 days before the initial pretrial conference; be ready to commit to trial settings. A party that joins new parties must give them all prior orders and the procedures manual. Criminal: responses are due within 10 days after the motion is filed and served, and a late response may be deemed a confession of the motion. Replies are due within 5 days after the response and at least 5 days before the hearing. Notify the court of a plea agreement at least 5 days before trial or risk costs.

docs.t: Judge Alan Bond Johnson (D. Wyo.) — Final pretrial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Alan Bond Johnson, D. Wyo.. Final pretrial (trap): The Joint Final Pretrial Memorandum (Appendix C form) is due 30 days before the final pretrial conference, which is usually about 4 weeks before trial. Plaintiff files it, and defendant must give plaintiff its final portion at least 3 business days before it is due; all counsel sign. Motions in limine are due with the memorandum. Written requests for authentication are due within 7 business days after an exhibit is made available; silence admits authenticity. Exhibit objections with copies and authority: the manual says at least 7 business days before trial, while the Appendix D order form says 10 business days. Deposition offers: notify opposing counsel 10 business days before trial, and objections or counter-designations are due 7 business days before trial, by page and line. Give the courtroom deputy a copy of each deposition to

docs.t: Judge Alan Bond Johnson (D. Wyo.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Alan Bond Johnson, D. Wyo.. Trial: Court usually sits 9:30 a.m. to about 5 p.m.; settings may be stacked. Plaintiff marks exhibits with numbers and defendant with letters; give the court 2 tabbed, indexed exhibit notebooks (or 2 identical drives if using electronic exhibits) and 4 copies of the witness list. Counsel speak from the podium. Do not pass exhibits to the jury without permission. Attorney voir dire is about 15 minutes per side. During deliberations, be within 15 minutes of the courtroom. Arrange Real Time transcription at least 3 weeks before trial; the Appendix D form asks counsel to send the court reporter witness and exhibit lists 10 days before trial. Bench trials: proposed findings and conclusions are due 30 days after the transcript is available, with record cites and covering elements, definitions, and damages. Offer the entire deposition as an exhibit, with a sum

docs.t: Judge Kelly H. Rankin (D. Wyo.) — Contacting chambers (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kelly H. Rankin, D. Wyo.. Contacting chambers (trap): Calls and emails about scheduling or procedure are allowed but must follow conferral and generally must be followed by a formal motion. Copy all counsel on every email, and get opposing counsel’s permission (or conference everyone in) before calling chambers. No faxes, and courtesy copies mailed or delivered to the clerk’s office are discouraged; file everything in CM/ECF except sealed documents, which go to the Clerk’s Office. Chambers pulls filings 24–48 hours after filing.

docs.t: Judge Kelly H. Rankin (D. Wyo.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Kelly H. Rankin, D. Wyo.. Motions: Every motion needs a proposed order, and a Word copy of it must be emailed to wyojudgekhr@wyd.uscourts.gov with all counsel copied. If a motion cites a deposition, email the relevant portion to chambers in E-Transcript or fully searchable PDF format. Non-dispositive motions usually go to the assigned magistrate judge; follow that judge’s procedures. For expedited treatment, get opposing counsel’s consent or move for an expedited schedule, with a proposed order.

docs.t: Judge Kelly H. Rankin (D. Wyo.) — Hearings and remote appearances (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kelly H. Rankin, D. Wyo.. Hearings and remote appearances (trap): Motions to dismiss are not set for hearing unless a party asks. At a granted hearing each side gets 30 minutes, shared among multiple parties on a side; plaintiff’s rebuttal comes out of its 30 minutes and must be reserved at the start. Telephone or video appearance is allowed only if the setting notice says so or the court grants leave: confer, then file a motion showing unusual circumstances at least 3 business days before the hearing (L.R. 83.5). If granted, arrange it with the courtroom deputy. The same applies to remote witnesses.

docs.t: Judge Kelly H. Rankin (D. Wyo.) — Discovery and experts (trap)
docs.x: Judge Kelly H. Rankin, D. Wyo.. Discovery and experts (trap): Do not file discovery notices in CM/ECF. The judge points counsel to the posted proportionality matrix for discovery requests. docs.t: Judge Kelly H. Rankin (D. Wyo.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Kelly H. Rankin, D. Wyo.. Case management: The joint case management plan (posted form) covers parties and parents for recusal, a 2-page-or-less case summary, jurisdiction (with every LLC member’s or partner’s citizenship in diversity cases), proportionality and ESI issues, and proposed dates. Consent to a magistrate judge should be fairly considered.

Failing to mark a foundation objection waives it, and a party forced to prove foundation over objection may seek fees and costs. Deposition designations go to opposing counsel 10 business days before trial; objections or counter-designations are due 5 business days before trial; unresolved differences must be reported to the court in writing 3 business days before trial. A party listing a will-call witness guarantees that witness’s presence. No remote witnesses without advance leave:

docs.t: Judge Kelly H. Rankin (D. Wyo.) — Exhibits and the court reporter
docs.x: Judge Kelly H. Rankin, D. Wyo.. docs.t: Judge Kelly H. Rankin (D. Wyo.) — Bench trials
docs.x: Judge Kelly H. Rankin, D. Wyo.. Bench trials: Direct testimony of experts and witnesses on significant technical matters (without significant credibility issues) is presented by unsworn narrative written statement, exchanged and filed 7 days before the final pretrial conference. The witness adopts it under oath, it is offered as an exhibit, and live supplementation and cross follow. Not used for adverse parties or subpoenaed witnesses; exhibits are not attached. Proposed findings and conclusions: the form order says plaintiff submits 14 days after trial ends (the form reads “at least fourteen (14) days after”) and defendant 14 days later, filed and emailed in Word. Plaintiff’s facts are numbered simple declarative sentences with no witness recitals or legal conclusions; defendant admits or denies each sentence by the same number.

docs.t: Judge Kelly H. Rankin (D. Wyo.) — Courtroom conduct
docs.x: Judge Kelly H. Rankin, D. Wyo.. Courtroom conduct: Counsel stay at the podium and must ask permission to approach the witness, bench, or jury; speak clearly into the microphone. Cellphones are not allowed in the courtroom, and no technology is allowed in the gallery without permission (L.R. 83.3). Counsel are strongly encouraged to use the electronic evidence presentation system and to arrange a pretrial tutorial with the courtroom deputy. Notify the court promptly when a case or motion settles, with a motion to vacate if appropriate.

docs.t: Judge Nancy D. Freudenthal (D. Wyo.) — Trial logistics
docs.x: Judge Nancy D. Freudenthal, D. Wyo.. Trial logistics: On the first day of a jury trial, report to chambers at 8:30 a.m. Trial days run 8:30 to 5:00. Openings are typically 30 minutes per side. Electronic exhibits go to the Clerk’s Office for JERS by 8:30 a.m. 5 days before trial (files up to 500MB each). No paper exhibit copies are needed; originals go to the deputy clerk as admitted. Send the court reporter a witness list 5 business days before trial (the Pointers say at least one week, with keyword indices); request real-time or daily copy 14 days ahead. docs.x: Judge Nancy D. Freudenthal, D. Wyo.. Courtroom conduct (trap): Stand to object and state the specific rule (for example, “irrelevant and inadmissible under Rule 402”); no speaking objections. Stay at the main podium unless permitted to approach; lavaliere microphones need permission. Mute counsel-table microphones during private conversations because jurors’ hearing devices pick them up. Only one attorney per party examines each witness, and the attorney who objects on direct handles cross and sidebar. Don’t greet witnesses or use first names. Expert reports are not admitted, nor are attorney-prepared charts of testimony unless the witness endorses them. Never make Golden Rule or “reptile” arguments, personal opinions, or appeals to a party’s wealth or ability to pay. During deliberations, be able to return within about 15 minutes and give the deputy two phone numbers.

docs.t: Judge Nancy D. Freudenthal (D. Wyo.) — Bench trials
docs.x: Judge Nancy D. Freudenthal, D. Wyo.. Bench trials: Each side files proposed findings and conclusions 5 business days before trial, emailed in Word, following the judge’s guidelines: numbered simple declarative sentences based on expected evidence, without testimony recitals, pejoratives, or legal conclusions, plus numbered legal conclusions with authority. Witness statements for experts and technical witnesses without significant credibility issues are exchanged and filed 7 days before the final pretrial conference. They are required for parties and witnesses under their control, but not for adverse parties or subpoenaed witnesses. The witness adopts the statement under oath, then may supplement live before cross.

docs.t: Judge Nancy D. Freudenthal (D. Wyo.) — Settlement and ADR
docs.x: Judge Nancy D. Freudenthal, D. Wyo.. Settlement and ADR: Consider mediation or a settlement conference well before the pre-dispositive-motion status conference. For court-assisted settlement, contact either of the District’s full-time magistrate judges.

docs.x: Judge Dale A. Drozd, E.D. Cal.. Briefs and page limits (trap): Times New Roman, no smaller than 12 point; footnotes no more than one size smaller than the text. docs.x: Judge Dale A. Drozd, E.D. Cal.. docs.x: Judge Dale A. Drozd, E.D. Cal.. docs.x: Judge Dale A. Drozd, E.D. Cal.. TROs, ex parte, and administrative relief: TROs and injunctions follow FRCP 65 and L.R. 231. Before filing, contact the courtroom deputy and the opposing party; state whether an opposition will be filed; and attach an affidavit explaining the need for the order, why a stipulation couldn’t be obtained, and why the matter can’t be noticed under L.R. 230. docs.x: Judge Dena M. Coggins, E.D. Cal.. Sealing and redaction: Nothing is sealed or redacted without prior approval, under L.R. 140 and 141. docs.x: Judge Dena M. Coggins, E.D. Cal.. docs.x: Judge Bernard A. Friedman, E.D. Mich.. Trial preparation (trap): Exchange exhibits at least 1 week before trial, numbered consecutively; a bench book is encouraged. Parties keep custody of their exhibits during trial and after trial pending appeal. Trial briefs must be exchanged before trial. Motions in limine are due no later than 1 week before trial and are generally heard the morning of trial. Joint jury instructions are filed at the beginning of trial. Bench trials: file proposed findings and conclusions before trial ends; findings are generally made orally.

docs.t: Judge Bernard A. Friedman (E.D. Mich.) — Jury selection and courtroom conduct
docs.x: Judge Bernard A. Friedman, E.D. Mich.. Jury selection and courtroom conduct: Striking method; the court conducts preliminary voir dire and allows reasonable voir dire by counsel, and challenges are handled so jurors do not know who excused them. In criminal cases two alternates are normally used and are not told they are alternates until the end. Only one lawyer per party may examine a given witness. Ask permission to approach the witness or bench; stand to speak, but you need not stay at the podium and may approach the jury box. Time limits on openings and closings are possible. The jury is charged before closing arguments and is given a copy of the instructions. Jurors typically may not take notes unless both sides agree.

docs.t: Judge Bernard A. Friedman (E.D. Mich.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Bernard A. Friedman, E.D. Mich.. Criminal cases: The court handles most pretrial matters, follows the court-rule cutoff dates, and enforces the standing orders’ discovery and motion cutoffs. Trial briefs are not always required; witness lists are preferred. The government is urged to disclose Jencks material before trial. Jury questionnaires are allowed in extraordinary cases, and instruction disputes are resolved at a hearing on the record.

docs.t: Judge Bernard A. Friedman (E.D. Mich.) — Pleas and sentencing
docs.x: Judge Bernard A. Friedman, E.D. Mich.. Pleas and sentencing: The court accepts Alford and nolo contendere pleas, sometimes over government objection, and will accept a plea agreement capping the sentence at a stated period above the bottom of the guideline range. A presentence report is required even with no custody and for corporate defendants, unless both sides waive it; if waived but the defendant asks for one, it will be ordered. Guideline disputes are typically resolved at sentencing, and a rejected Rule 11 agreement is announced in open court. Self-reporting may be allowed.

docs.t: Judge Brandy R. McMillion (E.D. Mich.) — Courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brandy R. McMillion, E.D. Mich.. Courtesy copies (trap): A paper courtesy copy of every motion and brief, with exhibits, must be mailed First-Class the day it is e-filed or hand-delivered by the next business day. It must be the e-filed document with the ECF stamp on each page, bound any way except a prong fastener (or 3-hole punched in a 3-ring binder); rubber bands and binder clips are not accepted. Label all exhibits and highlight the relevant portions. Include copies of the main cases and other authority relied on, with the relevant parts highlighted. Transcript or deposition exhibits must include the entire transcript, relevant portions highlighted, printed four pages per page and double-sided.

docs.t: Judge Brandy R. McMillion (E.D. Mich.) — Briefing and motion hearings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brandy R. McMillion, E.D. Mich.. Briefing and motion hearings (trap): Every brief needs a table of contents, a table of authorities, and an index, and references to the other side’s arguments must cite docket and page number. Sur-replies are generally not permitted. Strict compliance with L.R. 7.1(a) concurrence is required, and costs may be imposed. No briefing schedule is usually set; L.R. 7.1(e) deadlines apply. Extensions and requests for longer briefs (by concise stipulation and order or ex parte motion stating specific reasons) must be filed at least one week before the brief is due, and longer briefs are not routinely granted. The court often hears argument on civil motions (not pro se prisoner cases or reconsideration) and will notify the parties of the date; each side generally gets 15 minutes in total. If the parties resolve a pending motion, email the Case Manager by the

docs.t: Judge Brandy R. McMillion (E.D. Mich.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brandy R. McMillion, E.D. Mich.. Summary judgment (trap): Only one summary judgment motion per party without leave. The movant must file a Statement of Material Facts in short, numbered paragraphs, each with record citations; omitting it may get the motion struck or denied. The opponent must respond paragraph by paragraph with matching numbers and may add numbered additional facts; anything not specifically controverted is deemed admitted. Appendices must be indexed and tabbed. Skip boilerplate on the standard and string cites; focus on a few recent, controlling cases. Submit copies of unpublished or specialty-reporter opinions cited. Challenges to experts under FRE 702, 703, or 705 are due by the summary judgment deadline.

docs.t: Judge Brandy R. McMillion (E.D. Mich.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brandy R. McMillion, E.D. Mich.. Discovery disputes (trap): No discovery motion without leave. First meet and confer in good faith (an email exchange is not a meet and confer; failing to make yourself available may draw sanctions). Then email the Case Manager a brief summary to schedule a telephone conference with the court. At least 24 hours before the conference each side submits a one-page summary through the CM/ECF Utilities proposed-order link and exchanges it (as soon as possible if the call is set within 48 hours). If still unresolved, the court grants leave and decides the motion or refers it to the magistrate judge; the motion must attach the complete requests and responses, and a complete transcript for a deposition dispute. Noncompliance can draw costs and fees. Serve discovery early enough for responses before the cutoff; the court will not order discovery after it. The

docs.t: Judge Brandy R. McMillion (E.D. Mich.) — Protective orders and sealing
docs.x: Judge Brandy R. McMillion, E.D. Mich.. Protective orders and sealing: Stipulated protective orders are encouraged but must include the L.R. 5.3 language quoted on the page and may not authorize sealed filing in advance. Redaction is preferred over sealing. With any motion or stipulation to seal, submit a proposed order stating the particular reason, through the CM/ECF Utilities link; once granted, the movant files the documents electronically under seal.

docs.t: Judge Brandy R. McMillion (E.D. Mich.) — Contact, settlement, and TROs
docs.x: Judge Brandy R. McMillion, E.D. Mich.. Contact, settlement, and TROs: No ex parte communications. Direct administrative, procedural, scheduling, and case questions to the Case Manager (Leanne Hosking, 313-234-5146); no contact with law clerks unless authorized. Parties may request a status conference (telephone, video, or in person) at any time to resolve disputes. Notify chambers in writing by email by the next business day if a case settles. Interpreter and disability-accommodation requests are due at least 10 days before needed. Phone the Case Manager when filing a TRO or preliminary injunction motion; the court usually holds a prompt status conference and sets a schedule shorter than L.R. 7.1. Even ex parte TROs require some notice and a chance to be heard absent good cause, and TROs without notice are rarely granted.

docs.t: Judge Brandy R. McMillion (E.D. Mich.) — Admission, removal, and ADR
docs.x: Judge Brandy R. McMillion, E.D. Mich.. Admission, removal, and ADR: Pro hac vice admission is not permitted, and L.R. 83.20(f) local counsel (with an office in the district) is strictly enforced for bar members not active in the State Bar of Michigan. Removed cases are reviewed for jurisdiction, and an order to show cause issues if questions exist; the court does not remand sua sponte, and motions to remand for procedural defects are due within 30 days of removal. Parties may stipulate to case evaluation, mediation, or facilitation, or request a settlement conference, at any time. In every case the court holds a brief settlement status conference shortly after discovery closes.

docs.t: Judge Brandy R. McMillion (E.D. Mich.) — Scheduling conference
docs.x: Judge Brandy R. McMillion, E.D. Mich.. Scheduling conference: The court reviews the Rule 26(f) report after an answer and either enters a scheduling order or sets a (telephonic) scheduling conference. The joint Case Management Report/Discovery Plan is due 7 days before the conference and must address 11 agenda items under separate headings (related cases, jurisdiction, facts, legal issues, amendments, discovery, ESI, settlement, magistrate consent, trial, miscellaneous), stating each side’s position on any disagreement. Discovery may begin after the meet and confer. Expert disclosures are due no later than 90 days before trial and Rule 26(a)(3) pretrial disclosures no later than 30 days before trial, unless the order sets other dates.

docs.t: Judge Brandy R. McMillion (E.D. Mich.) — Civil final pretrial and trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brandy R. McMillion, E.D. Mich.. Civil final pretrial and trial (trap): Trial counsel, individual parties, and representatives with full settlement authority (including insurers and government entities) must attend the final pretrial conference. The Joint Final Pretrial Order (strictly per L.R. 16.2) is due through CM/ECF utilities 2 weeks before the conference. A Joint Bench Book and courtesy exhibit binders are due 1 week before the conference. The bench book includes an administrative section (trial length in half-day blocks), a joint theory of the case read to the jury, up to 15 case-specific voir dire questions plus a 2–3 paragraph joint statement of the case, witness lists with examination times, agreed and disputed jury instructions and verdict form, evidentiary issues, trial briefs, and (bench trials) proposed findings. Also e-file the stipulated instructions and email Word

docs.x: Judge Brandy R. McMillion, E.D. Mich.. Criminal cases (trap): The government must immediately report whether the case or investigation was opened in the E.D. Mich. Counsel meet within 10 days of arraignment; on request the government provides Rule 16(a)(1) material and Brady/Giglio evidence (a signed list of it), or moves for relief within that period. docs.x: Judge David M. Lawson, E.D. Mich.. Concurrence and motion format (trap): L.R. 5.1, 7.1, and the ECF policies are strictly enforced; noncompliance likely means denial and possible sanctions. Failure to comply with L.R. 7.1(a) usually results in dismissal of the motion. Motions must be clear and succinct. Citations go in the text, not footnotes, and follow the latest Bluebook; footnotes are discouraged and must be the same size as the text (at least 14 point proportional). Briefs need a concise statement of facts with record cites under ECF Rule 6. Do not combine a response with a counter-motion (ECF Rule R5(e)). In criminal cases, select only your own client when e-filing, not all defendants.

docs.x: Judge David M. Lawson, E.D. Mich.. docs.t: Judge David M. Lawson (E.D. Mich.) — Summary judgment, experts, and patent cases
docs.x: Judge David M. Lawson, E.D. Mich.. Summary judgment, experts, and patent cases: Only one summary judgment motion per party without leave, and challenges to several counts must be in a single motion. docs.x: Judge David M. Lawson, E.D. Mich.. Sealing and protective orders (trap): File a motion for leave (after seeking concurrence) before docketing anything under seal. Agreed protective orders are encouraged: e-file a stipulation and send the proposed order through Utilities. The stipulation must include the judge’s required “Filing Under Seal” language (no advance sealing authority; motion under L.R. 5.3 and Shane Group) and a provision requiring notice to the designating party before filing its confidential material.

docs.t: Judge David M. Lawson (E.D. Mich.) — Stipulations, contact, and settlement notice

Contact the case manager or judicial assistant only on procedural and scheduling matters; contacting law clerks is discouraged. Report a settlement in writing by email or fax by the next business day.

docs.t: Judge David M. Lawson (E.D. Mich.) — Scheduling and discovery

docs.x: Judge David M. Lawson, E.D. Mich.. Removal and TROs: Many removed cases get a standing order requiring the removing party, within 7 days, to explain any missing joinder, timeliness, forum-defendant issues, full citizenship of all parties (including members of non-corporate entities), the amount in controversy, or the federal basis. Plaintiff may respond within 14 court days. Remand motions for procedural defects are due within 30 days of removal. TROs without notice are rarely granted absent a true emergency where notice would cause the harm. Call the case manager on filing an injunction motion.

Trial counsel, natural-person parties, a representative of other parties, and any controlling insurer must attend in person with “full authority,” meaning authority exceeding plaintiff’s last demand; phone availability does not count, and Rule 16(f) sanctions apply. Motions in limine are generally due 5 weeks before the final pretrial conference. R. 2.403, including sanctions; facili

docs.t: Judge David M. Lawson (E.D. Mich.) — Trial submissions
docs.x: Judge David M. Lawson, E.D. Mich.. Trial submissions: At least 1 week before trial: stipulated jury instructions (no boilerplate; the court’s standard instructions are available from the case manager) with Word-compatible media certified virus free, separately filed disputed instructions, voir dire requests, a statement of claims or defenses of no more than 2 pages, witness and exhibit lists on the court’s form, and optional trial briefs (mandatory in bench trials). Bench trials: proposed findings and conclusions at least 1 week before trial, one fact per paragraph with exhibit or testimony citations, plus a Word copy.

docs.t: Judge David M. Lawson (E.D. Mich.) — Trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge David M. Lawson, E.D. Mich.. Trial (trap): Trials run Monday through Friday; jury trials generally begin Tuesday. After day one, trial usually runs 8 a.m. to about 2 p.m. with two 15-minute breaks (occasionally 8:30–12:30 and 1:45–5). Deliver the exhibit book 1 day before trial. Documents and photos must be published electronically, with two hard-copy sets (court and jury). All counsel and assistants must schedule a joint technology tutorial with the court’s IT staff at least 1 week before trial. Show opening-statement exhibits to opposing counsel in advance. The court conducts initial voir dire and usually allows probative follow-up by counsel; peremptories alternate. Evidentiary stipulations must be in writing, signed by counsel (and the defendant in criminal cases). Purge deposition testimony of objections well before trial. Jurors may take notes but may not question witnesses.

Rule 11(c)(1)(B) and (C) agreements are acceptable. The defendant must attend all hearings and the final pretrial conference, and writs must be submitted 4 weeks ahead. Stand-in counsel at the final pretrial conference is not allowed except in extraordinary circumstances with permission and client consent. Witness lists, voir dire, stipulated instructions, and exhibit lists go directly to chambers, not e-filed, usually 1 week before trial; a defense-theory instruction is due on the first day of trial. docs.x: Judge Denise Page Hood, E.D. Mich.. Courtesy copies (trap): Send chambers a courtesy copy of all motions, dispositive and non-dispositive, plus responses, replies, and all exhibits. Bind on the left side (no rubber bands or binder clips), use exhibit labels that extend beyond the side of the paper, and attach a printed Notice of Electronic Filing to the front. Mail it first class the same day you e-file. If the filing relates to a proceeding within the next 5 days or otherwise needs immediate attention, hand-deliver it to chambers by the morning of the next business day. docs.x: Judge Denise Page Hood, E.D. Mich.. Motions and concurrence (trap): L.R. 5.1, L.R. 7.1, and the Electronic Filing Policies and Procedures are strictly enforced for all motions. If no conversation occurs, the motion must specifically describe the reasonable efforts made; the outcome of the conference must be stated, and all of it documented specifically in the motion papers. Hearings are held on most motions, usually on Wednesday afternoons.

docs.t: Judge Denise Page Hood (E.D. Mich.) — Conferences
docs.x: Judge Denise Page Hood, E.D. Mich.. Conferences: A Rule 16(b) scheduling conference is held after the answer is filed; the scheduling order and a standing order on the Joint Final Pretrial Order issue then. Status conferences are set case by case. Conferences are generally held on Monday afternoons. Out-of-state counsel may attend scheduling and status conferences (but not pretrial or settlement conferences) by telephone if arranged in advance. Parties generally must attend pretrial and settlement conferences.

docs.t: Judge Denise Page Hood (E.D. Mich.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Denise Page Hood, E.D. Mich.. Discovery: The court usually allows 4–6 months for discovery. docs.x: Judge Denise Page Hood, E.D. Mich.. TROs and injunctions: The court follows Fed. R. Civ. P. 65 and grants ex parte relief only in extraordinary circumstances. Briefing is typically accelerated, and hearings are set as the urgency requires.

docs.t: Judge Denise Page Hood (E.D. Mich.) — Removal
docs.x: Judge Denise Page Hood, E.D. Mich.. Removal: If jurisdiction is questionable, the court issues an order to show cause or waits for a motion to remand. It will not dismiss or remand sua sponte without notice to the parties.

docs.t: Judge Denise Page Hood (E.D. Mich.) — Final pretrial and settlement (trap)
docs.x: Judge Denise Page Hood, E.D. Mich.. The judge routinely takes part in settlement talks in jury cases and refers non-jury cases to another judge or a magistrate judge for a settlement conference. The form order may refer a case to Wayne County Mediation, and no motions other than motions in limine may be filed after the motion cutoff.

Discovery motions are generally referred to the magistrate judge (no blanket referral); after referral, communicate only with that chambers. The court will not order discovery after the cutoff. Discovery may be extended by stipulation, before or after the cutoff and without a motion, only if the motion cutoff, final pretrial conference, and trial dates are unaffected; other changes need a timely written motion. The court may take telephone calls on disputes arising during a deposition.

docs.t: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds (E.D. Mich.) — Conferences, removal, and TROs
docs.x: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds, E.D. Mich.. Conferences, removal, and TROs: A scheduling conference sets cutoffs and pretrial, trial, pretrial-order, and instruction dates. Status and pretrial conferences may be by telephone for out-of-town counsel, and otherwise with prior approval. The court does not remand sua sponte (L.R. 81.1); an order to show cause issues if removal looks improper, and oral argument is typically held on remand motions. For TROs and preliminary injunctions, the court consults counsel and sets a shortened schedule by written order.

docs.t: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds (E.D. Mich.) — Mediation and settlement
docs.x: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds, E.D. Mich.. Mediation and settlement: Diversity cases are not routinely sent to L.R. 16.3 mediation; referral occurs after the discovery cutoff only if the parties stipulate to mediation sanctions, by the scheduling-order date, and counsel must complete mediation before the final pretrial conference. The judge routinely participates in settlement in jury cases and refers non-jury cases to another judge. Settlement is discussed at the final pretrial conference, and a settlement conference can be requested at any stage.

docs.t: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds (E.D. Mich.) — Final pretrial order and conference (trap)
docs.x: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds, E.D. Mich.. Final pretrial order and conference (trap): Counsel confer face to face; plaintiff drafts the joint final pretrial order under L.R. 16.2. The scheduling order requires it at least 1 week before the final pretrial conference, with an original and one copy to chambers. Pending motions needing pretrial decision must be flagged by then. Witness-list additions are allowed only in exceptional circumstances. Parties must attend the final pretrial conference with trial counsel, who must have full authority to discuss settlement without further client approval, unless other arrangements are approved in advance. The conference is typically 1 to 2 weeks before trial. Foundation or authenticity objections not raised before trial are waived.

docs.t: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds (E.D. Mich.) — Trial submissions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds, E.D. Mich.. Trial submissions (trap): Motions in limine: the page says at the final pretrial conference or 2 weeks before trial, whichever comes first; the scheduling order says 1 week before the trial term. Jury instructions: the page says the court gives counsel its standard opening and closing instructions at the final pretrial conference, and the joint instructions, joint verdict form, and separate disputed instructions (with each side’s support or objection) are due on the first day of trial, on paper and electronically. The scheduling order instead requires stipulated instructions 1 week before trial. At least 1 week before trial: voir dire requests and a statement of claims or defenses of no more than 2 pages. Bench trials: proposed findings and conclusions are filed before trial (the order says 1 week before), on paper and electronically.

docs.t: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds (E.D. Mich.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds, E.D. Mich.. Trial: Trailing docket; report trial conflicts as soon as discovered (the earliest notice has priority). Hours are set week by week. Openings and closings are limited to 30–60 minutes, and repetitive or cumulative evidence may be limited. Ask permission to approach a witness or the bench; bench conferences are discouraged. Exchange exhibits 1 week before trial; bench book required. The page says plaintiff numbers from 1 and defendant from 500 (the order says each party starts at 1); traditional stickers preferred. Parties keep custody of exhibits during trial and pending appeal. Resolve evidentiary and foundation issues before trial; do not bring record keepers when business-record authenticity is not really disputed. Trial will not be adjourned for last-minute depositions.

docs.t: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds (E.D. Mich.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds, E.D. Mich.. Jury selection: Strike method; the court conducts voir dire with limited follow-up by counsel, and counsel may not ask about the amount of damages sought. Three peremptories per party in civil cases, exercised in open court; a pass counts as an exercise. No alternates in civil trials; all seated jurors deliberate. The jury is charged before closing arguments and gets copies of the instructions. Juror questionnaires are allowed on motion for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds (E.D. Mich.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Nancy G. Edmunds, E.D. Mich.. Criminal cases: One or two alternates; defendant 10 peremptories, government 6. Pretrial conferences and arraignments on information are typically referred to a magistrate judge. Trial briefs are welcome but not required, and early Jencks disclosure is urged. Alford and nolo contendere pleas are rare and never accepted over government objection. Guideline disputes are typically resolved at a hearing before sentencing, and self-reporting is typically permitted.

docs.t: Judge Paul D. Borman (E.D. Mich.) — Courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Paul D. Borman, E.D. Mich.. Courtesy copies (trap): Courtesy hard copies are always required. Under the case management order, deliver a copy of all motions and briefs to chambers by first-class mail or hand delivery the same day you e-file. Copies must be one-sided, with tabbed exhibits and an index of exhibits, and bound so the CM/ECF header shows on every page. No top fasteners, prong fasteners, side staples, loose pages, or single binder clips; a three-ring binder is preferred, though a short filing may be stapled in the top left corner or bound on the side. Staple the motion and brief separately from the exhibits, and start the brief on a separate page.

docs.t: Judge Paul D. Borman (E.D. Mich.) — Briefs and format (trap)
docs.x: Judge Paul D. Borman, E.D. Mich.. Briefs and format (trap): All filings, including exhibits, must be in 14-point font (L.R. 5.1(a)(3)). Every motion, response, and reply must include a table of contents, a table of authorities, and an index. Cite deposition testimony by page and line and attach the entire transcript, printed one page per page, with the relevant passages highlighted. File the full text of any unpublished source in an indexed appendix with the relevant portion highlighted or underlined. No string citations without at least parenthetical explanation; focus on a few recent, controlling cases. Ex parte applications to exceed 25 pages are rarely granted.

docs.t: Judge Paul D. Borman (E.D. Mich.) — Motion practice
docs.x: Judge Paul D. Borman, E.D. Mich.. Motion practice: Strict compliance with L.R. 7.1(a) concurrence; the court will strike papers and impose costs for noncompliance. L.R. 7.1(d) and (e) response deadlines are enforced, and the court sends notice of any hearing. If the parties resolve an issue in a pending motion, notify the court immediately by email to the case manager or fax to chambers. Proposed and stipulated orders go through CM/ECF Utilities/Proposed Orders and are not docketed. TROs and preliminary injunctions: the court sets the schedule and, absent extraordinary circumstances, requires some notice to the other side and a chance for both sides to be heard. Conferring first is strongly encouraged.

docs.t: Judge Paul D. Borman (E.D. Mich.) — Summary judgment and expert challenges (trap)
docs.x: Judge Paul D. Borman, E.D. Mich.. Summary judgment and expert challenges (trap): Absent extraordinary circumstances shown by motion, summary judgment motions may be filed only after fact and expert discovery close, and only one per party, addressing all counts within the page limits. Challenges to experts under Rules 702, 703, or 705 are due no later than the summary judgment deadline (typically 45 days after all discovery closes).

docs.t: Judge Paul D. Borman (E.D. Mich.) — Discovery and scheduling
docs.x: Judge Paul D. Borman, E.D. Mich.. Discovery and scheduling: Typical schedule: initial disclosures 45 days after the Rule 26(f) conference; amendments 30 days after the scheduling order; fact discovery 6–9 months; witness lists exchanged and proponent expert disclosures 60 days before the fact cutoff; rebuttal expert disclosures 30 days before; expert discovery closes 45 days after the fact cutoff. Start discovery once the case is joined; don’t wait for a scheduling order. Extending the cutoff takes a motion or stipulation to the district judge, and approval should not be presumed. L.R. 37.1 is strictly enforced. Discovery motions and deposition disputes usually go to the assigned magistrate judge; once referred, direct all communication to that judge’s chambers.

docs.t: Judge Paul D. Borman (E.D. Mich.) — Motions in limine (trap)
docs.x: Judge Paul D. Borman, E.D. Mich.. Motions in limine (trap): Due typically 60 days before the final pretrial conference. Each motion must state that the conference occurred and that the parties were absolutely unable to resolve the issue.

docs.t: Judge Paul D. Borman (E.D. Mich.) — Final pretrial order (trap)

Meeting and conferring on the legal basis of every exhibit objection before the conference is mandatory, and the court will ask about it. Only listed witnesses and exhibits are allowed, absent rebuttal or good cause. The parties themselves (natural persons and representatives of other parties) must attend the final pretrial conference with full settlement authority. Corporate parties must file a statement of parents and 10% owners, and LLCs must identify every member, including members of me

docs.x: Judge Paul D. Borman, E.D. Mich.. Trial (trap): Trials usually run 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., with time limits on openings and closings and possibly on the whole trial. Number exhibits in advance (plaintiff from 100, defendant from 500) with exhibit stickers, and don’t highlight or mark them. Counsel keep custody of exhibits and must have them in order when deliberations begin. Voir dire requests and a one-paragraph statement of each party’s claim or defense are due 1 week before trial; the court conducts voir dire with limited follow-up by counsel. Civil juries a

docs.t: Judge Paul D. Borman (E.D. Mich.) — ERISA benefits cases
docs.x: Judge Paul D. Borman, E.D. Mich.. ERISA benefits cases: Review is on the administrative record under Wilkins, and Rule 56 procedures are not used. Each party files a “Statement of Procedural Challenge” or “Statement of No Procedural Challenge” 3 weeks after the order; a procedural challenge suspends later deadlines pending a conference on limited discovery. Defendant serves the administrative record (with the plan and summary plan description) in 3 weeks; standard-of-review statements are due in 1 month; cross-motions to reverse or affirm, with a joint appendix, are due in 4 months; responses 1 month later and replies 2 weeks after that. Deliver a single bound courtesy copy at e-filing (not with a top hole-punch binder).

docs.t: Judge Paul D. Borman (E.D. Mich.) — Criminal and compassionate release
docs.x: Judge Paul D. Borman, E.D. Mich.. Criminal and compassionate release: Pretrial matters are generally not referred to a magistrate judge. The court may accept Alford or nolo contendere pleas, always requires a presentence report, and enforces a firm plea cutoff. Criminal juries are generally 14; juror questionnaires may be allowed in high-profile or complex cases; peremptory allocation in multi-defendant trials is set at the final pretrial conference. No criminal trial brief is required, and the government is urged to disclose Jencks material before trial. Compassionate release exhibits must be numbered sequentially across the whole packet, indexed by exhibit, category, and page numbers, and highlighted on the relevant material.

docs.t: Judge Paul D. Borman (E.D. Mich.) — Other
docs.x: Judge Paul D. Borman, E.D. Mich.. Other: The court often refers civil cases to facilitation. Local counsel is required for attorneys who are not members of the State Bar of Michigan. Fed. R. Civ. P. 55(a) is strictly followed before a default judgment. If removal looks improper, the court issues an order to show cause or dismisses a facially invalid removal petition, and may hear argument.

docs.t: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland (E.D. Mich.) — Jurisdiction review (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland, E.D. Mich.. Jurisdiction review (trap): The court reviews jurisdiction in every case. In a diversity case that does not plead each party’s citizenship or the amount in controversy, expect an order to show cause why the case should not be dismissed or remanded. Raise jurisdictional objections as soon as possible.

docs.t: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland (E.D. Mich.) — Scheduling conference
docs.x: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland, E.D. Mich.. Scheduling conference: A Notice of Scheduling Conference issues when the Answer is filed. If 3 weeks pass after the Answer without a notice, call the case manager. The conference is off the record in chambers in Port Huron, with trial counsel; responsible parties are occasionally required, and a phone conference is sometimes allowed. If trial counsel cannot attend, substitute counsel with complete working knowledge and decision authority must appear; a new date can sometimes be arranged with the case manager.

docs.t: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland (E.D. Mich.) — Rule 26(f) plan (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland, E.D. Mich.. Rule 26(f) plan (trap): Plaintiff must organize the meet-and-confer and file a Rule 26(f)(3) plan at least 7 days before the conference. Corporate parties must file the LR 83.4 disclosure statement at least 7 days before it. Come prepared, after consulting clients, to narrow the issues, including withdrawing without prejudice claims and defenses not presently sustainable (the notice stresses that “failure to state a claim” is not a defense), and to state each claim’s and defense’s elements and good-faith factual basis. Also address entity parties, jurisdiction, related cases, amendments, experts, discovery, the Model ESI Order, ADR, consent, bench trial, dispositive motions, and settlement.

docs.t: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland (E.D. Mich.) — Suggested plan outline
docs.x: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland, E.D. Mich.. Suggested plan outline: The court’s sample outline asks for summaries of claims and defenses (not reprinted pleadings), any claims or defenses withdrawn without prejudice, a discovery plan, and the case’s complexity tier. It requires a discovery budget: each side’s estimated discovery costs, including attorney fees, with counsel stating the client was specifically advised and approved. Include an estimate of in-court hours for each side; the outline notes an ordinary personal-injury case should need about 20 hours. In a non-jury case, do not reveal strategy that could affect the court’s impartiality.

docs.t: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland (E.D. Mich.) — Discovery timelines
docs.x: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland, E.D. Mich.. Discovery timelines: Simple case: discovery closes about 2 to 3 months after it starts, with resolution in under a year from the Answer. Standard case: 4 to 5 months, about one year. Complex case: 6 to 8 months, under two years. Highly complex case: at the court’s discretion, with counsel invited to propose a timeline. Counsel are encouraged to begin Rule 26(a)(1) disclosures and discovery by mutual consent before the conference.

docs.t: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland (E.D. Mich.) — Magistrate judge consent
docs.x: Judge Robert Hardy Cleland, E.D. Mich.. Magistrate judge consent: The court will consider unanimous consent to full magistrate-judge jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 636(c) and Rule 73, using the standard consent form. The notice points out that magistrate judges have no felony trials, so an earlier and more certain trial date is likely.

docs.t: Judge Robert J. White (E.D. Mich.) — Contacting chambers
docs.x: Judge Robert J. White, E.D. Mich.. Contacting chambers: The court strongly prefers email to the case manager, Tara Villereal (Tara_Villereal@mied.uscourts.gov), with opposing counsel copied. To adjourn a date, confer first and send a single email listing agreed dates that work for everyone. Ex parte contact with the case manager is allowed only on scheduling or administrative matters; contact with law clerks needs the court’s express approval. Counsel may ask the case manager for a telephone, Zoom, or Teams status conference to resolve disputes without motion practice.

docs.t: Judge Robert J. White (E.D. Mich.) — Brief format and certification (trap)

More than 10 footnotes means the brief is stricken; case and statute citations go inline. Every fact statement needs a pincite. The first party to cite a document attaches all of it, and others cite the docketed copy as (ECF No. ##, PageID.###-###). Do not attach unpublished cases available on Westlaw or Lexis, and do not file a motion inside a response brief without permission.

docs.t: Judge Robert J. White (E.D. Mich.) — Courtesy copies (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert J. White, E.D. Mich.. Courtesy copies (trap): Mail a courtesy copy only if a brief and its exhibits total 50 or more pages: the e-filed version with CM/ECF headers, spiral or three-ring bound, printed single-sided, with exhibits tabbed.

docs.t: Judge Robert J. White (E.D. Mich.) — Motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert J. White, E.D. Mich.. Motions (trap): Excess pages are discouraged; seek them by motion for leave at least one day before the deadline for fewer than five pages and at least one week before for five or more, or the motion may be struck or denied. Responses and replies follow L.R. 7.1(e) unless the court says otherwise; a motion without a timely response is treated as unopposed. Motions to amend must attach a redlined proposed pleading (L.R. 15.1). Leave is required for more than one summary judgment motion (L.R. 7.1(b)).

docs.t: Judge Robert J. White (E.D. Mich.) — Summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert J. White, E.D. Mich.. Summary judgment (trap): The supporting brief must begin with a “Statement of Material Facts” in numbered paragraphs with record citations. The opposition must begin with a “Counter-statement of Material Facts” using matching numbers, admitting or contesting each fact with record citations, and may add a separately headed “Statement of Additional Material Facts.” If additional facts are raised, the reply must begin with a “Reply to Counter-statement of Material Facts” using the opponent’s numbering. All of these statements count toward the page limit.

docs.t: Judge Robert J. White (E.D. Mich.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert J. White, E.D. Mich.. Discovery disputes (trap): No discovery motion until: (1) a good-faith meet and confer (an email exchange is not enough; refusing to make yourself available may draw sanctions); (2) an email to the case manager requesting a telephone conference, with a concise summary and a certification that step 1 is done, and each side’s one-page summary exchanged and submitted through CM/ECF Utilities at least 24 hours before; (3) only then a motion, which the court decides or refers to the magistrate judge. The motion must attach the complete requests and responses and, for a completed deposition, the full (not minuscript) transcript. Noncompliance can draw costs and fees. Stipulated protective orders go through CM/ECF Utilities, must reference L.R. 5.3, and may not pre-authorize sealed filings; redaction is preferred. The discovery cutoff may be extended by stipul

docs.x: Judge Robert J. White, E.D. Mich..
