Experts and summary judgment: Expert designations, for retained and non-retained experts alike, must come with an expert affidavit (all opinions and bases, data considered, exhibits, qualifications with 10 years of publications, compensation, and 4 years of prior testimony); experts may testify only to what it contains. Treating physicians may instead produce their files but need a full designation for opinions beyond treatment. Dispositive motions must have a separate section of individually numbered facts, and oppositions must begin with a concise list of the material facts claimed to be genuinely disputed. Comply with Local Rules 7.1 and 56.1.

docs.t: Judge Gary A. Fenner (W.D. Mo.) — Pretrial filings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Gary A. Fenner, W.D. Mo.. Pretrial filings (trap): Motions in limine at least 10 days before the pretrial conference, responses at least 3 days before. At least 3 days before: stipulation of uncontroverted facts, stipulation as to admissibility, witness lists, and exhibit lists, with an exhibit index for the courtroom deputy and each exhibit marked when listed. Deposition designations by parties asserting claims 10 days before the conference; objections and counter-designations at least 5 days before. Unlisted witnesses and exhibits are excluded absent leave for good cause, and a preserved request to stipulate counts as a Rule 36 request for admission.

docs.t: Judge Gary A. Fenner (W.D. Mo.) — Jury cases before trial
docs.x: Judge Gary A. Fenner, W.D. Mo.. Jury cases before trial: Two weeks before trial, jointly file clean and annotated proposed jury instructions (Eighth Circuit models and/or MAI, unlabeled by party) and email both, as separate Word documents, to the courtroom deputy and law clerk. Objections with authority and alternative instructions are due 1 week before trial. Proposed voir dire questions at least 10 days before trial; objections to the other side’s at least 5 days before. Optional trial briefs at least 5 days before trial.

docs.t: Judge Gary A. Fenner (W.D. Mo.) — Bench trials
docs.x: Judge Gary A. Fenner, W.D. Mo.. Bench trials: Proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law are required at least 5 days before trial, with a Word copy emailed to the courtroom deputy and law clerk at filing. Optional trial briefs are due at least 5 days before trial.

docs.t: Judge Gary A. Fenner (W.D. Mo.) — Trial rules
docs.x: Judge Gary A. Fenner, W.D. Mo.. Trial rules: Openings 30 minutes per side. Direct of non-party fact witnesses is capped at 60 minutes, cross no longer than direct, redirect 20 minutes, and recross no longer than redirect; seek any change for good cause at the earliest opportunity, usually by the pretrial conference. In jury trials the court conducts initial voir dire, then each side gets no more than 15 minutes of its own questions. At most 2 experts per party per subject, and do not ask to have a witness declared an expert. Show opposing counsel any visual aid and get agreement before using it in opening. Approach witnesses without asking, but question from a reasonable distance; witnesses stay in the witness chair unless leave is given. State objections by legal ground only. Each party must fax a description of the dispute, no more than one page, to the court at 417-865-2618 and to opposing counsel at least 24 hours before the teleconference.

docs.t: Judge M. Douglas Harpool (W.D. Mo.) — Discovery conduct and ESI
docs.x: Judge M. Douglas Harpool, W.D. Mo.. Discovery conduct and ESI: Counsel are ordered to cooperate, communicate regularly, treat everyone professionally, and reply promptly to opposing counsel. Review the court’s Principles for the Discovery of ESI before the Rule 26(f) conference and discuss its Checklist at the conference. Discovery must be completed, not just served, by the deadline, and the court reserves control over depositions.

docs.t: Judge M. Douglas Harpool (W.D. Mo.) — Experts and Daubert (trap)
docs.x: Judge M. Douglas Harpool, W.D. Mo.. Experts and Daubert (trap): Expert designations cover anyone giving Rule 702, 703, or 705 testimony, retained or not, and must come with an affidavit (all opinions and bases, data considered, exhibits, qualifications with 10 years of publications, compensation, and 4 years of prior testimony). Testimony is limited to the report and any deposition. Treating physicians may instead produce their files, but testimony is limited to them unless added opinions are disclosed by affidavit or deposition. Experts must be made available for deposition in order of disclosure and within 30 days, unless agreed otherwise. Daubert motions have their own deadline (the in limine deadline does not apply), and missing it waives Daubert arguments.

docs.t: Judge M. Douglas Harpool (W.D. Mo.) — Business records
docs.x: Judge M. Douglas Harpool, W.D. Mo.. Business records: Notify all parties by the set deadline of any business records you intend to self-authenticate under FRE 803(6), 902(11), and 902(12), and file a certificate of service showing compliance.

Motions to extend under Rules 6(b), 31, 33, 34, or 36 must state the original due date, the number of prior extensions and when the last expires, the cause and why the action isn’t done, and whether opposing counsel agrees (agreement does not bind the court).

docs.t: Judge M. Douglas Harpool (W.D. Mo.) — Mediation (MAP)

See Section V of the MAP General Order for extensions.

docs.t: Judge Megan Blair Benton (W.D. Mo.) — Trial brief and time limits
docs.x: Judge Megan Blair Benton, W.D. Mo.. Trial brief and time limits: A trial brief is optional, due 5 business days before trial under the sample orders (5 days before the pretrial conference under the guidelines), and should address important evidentiary issues. The court may set time limits on openings and on direct and cross of all witnesses, and counsel should be ready to justify their trial-length estimate. The pretrial conference and trial date change only by leave of court.

docs.x: Judge Roseann Ambrosia Ketchmark, W.D. Mo.. Discovery disputes (trap): Any discovery motion filed without complying with Local Rule 37.1 will be denied. For a teleconference, call the court at 816-512-5110 and follow the Discovery Dispute Protocol. The requesting party sends opposing counsel a 1–2 page description of the dispute, the efforts to resolve it, and both sides’ legal positions; opposing counsel answers in 1–2 pages, and a 1-page reply is allowed only if entirely new issues are raised. Confer early on deadlines for these exchanges. At least 24 hours before the call, the requesting party submits the description, response, and any reply to the court, together with the specific discovery request and objection if one is at issue.

docs.t: Judge Roseann Ambrosia Ketchmark (W.D. Mo.) — Summary judgment and experts
docs.x: Judge Roseann Ambrosia Ketchmark, W.D. Mo.. Summary judgment and experts: Summary judgment motions must comply with Local Rules 7.0 and 56.1. The response and the reply must restate each statement of fact and additional fact, using the original paragraph number, immediately before admitting or denying it. Experts include fact witnesses giving expert opinions. Rule 26(a)(2)(B) experts must provide an affidavit with the Rule 26(a)(2)(B)(i)–(vi) disclosures and may testify only to its contents absent leave. Treating physicians may produce their files instead, but need the affidavit to testify beyond the treatment provided.

docs.x: Judge Roseann Ambrosia Ketchmark, W.D. Mo.. MAP mediation must occur within 75 days after the Rule 26(f) conference; cases with an outside mediator must file the designation of mediator within 14 days after it. Scheduling and ECF questions go to the courtroom deputy, LaTandra Wheeler (816-512-5629); other questions to a law clerk (816-512-5110). Don’t send attorney-to-attorney communications to the court, and confer with opposing counsel before asking for a conference or ruling. Handing papers to chambers staff is not filing.

docs.t: Judge Roseann Ambrosia Ketchmark (W.D. Mo.) — Jury selection, openings, and juror questions
docs.x: Judge Roseann Ambrosia Ketchmark, W.D. Mo.. Jury selection, openings, and juror questions: If the parties agree, the attorneys may conduct voir dire and give brief openings at the start of voir dire; otherwise the court conducts voir dire and allows brief follow-up by each side. If the parties agree, the jury is instructed on the law before openings. There is generally no time limit on openings. Jurors may take notes and may submit written questions after counsel finish with each witness; every juror turns in a card. The court reviews questions with counsel at the bench, where counsel may object or ask to revise the form. A criminal defendant who testifies may choose whether juror questions may be asked of the defendant.

docs.t: Judge Colleen D. Holland (W.D.N.Y.) — Motions and oral argument
docs.x: Judge Colleen D. Holland, W.D.N.Y.. Motions and oral argument: Unless the court has already given a date, motions must not contain return dates. The court generally enters a motion scheduling order; if none is entered, the default deadlines in Local Rules of Civil Procedure 5.5 and 7 and Local Rule of Criminal Procedure 12 apply. Oral argument is not held on every motion; the court schedules it when argument may help resolve the motion.

docs.x: Judge Colleen D. Holland, W.D.N.Y.. Courtesy copies (trap): Judge Holland requires courtesy copies of motion papers filed in CM/ECF. Voluminous copies should be three-hole punched, tabbed, and placed in three-ring binders.

docs.x: Judge Colleen D. Holland, W.D.N.Y.. Page limits and citations (trap): To exceed the page limits in Local Rule of Civil Procedure 7 or Local Rule of Criminal Procedure 12, send a letter request to chambers, copied to all counsel and self-represented parties, at least one business day before the filing deadline, stating the number of additional pages requested. Put citations to legal authority in the text of memoranda of law, not in footnotes.

docs.t: Judge Colleen D. Holland (W.D.N.Y.) — Adjournments and extensions
docs.x: Judge Colleen D. Holland, W.D.N.Y.. Adjournments and extensions: A schedule may be modified only for good cause and with the court’s consent. When the parties agree, send a letter request to Judge Holland; no formal motion is needed. Without opposing counsel’s consent, a motion must be filed. Criminal: e-file letter requests as a motion on CM/ECF, and address exclusion of time under the Speedy Trial Act. Civil: send letter requests by mail, email (holland@nywd.uscourts.gov), fax, or hand delivery.

docs.t: Judge Colleen D. Holland (W.D.N.Y.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Colleen D. Holland, W.D.N.Y.. Discovery disputes (trap): Before any motion, raise the dispute by letter of no more than four single-spaced pages, copied to all counsel and self-represented parties, sent by mail, email, fax, or hand delivery. Judge Holland will generally schedule a conference to try to resolve it informally; if that fails, the parties may file a formal motion. The letter process is not expedited motion practice: give a brief overview with supporting documentation and each side’s position. Arguments are not waived by leaving them out of the letter.

docs.t: Judge Colleen D. Holland (W.D.N.Y.) — Telephone participation
docs.x: Judge Colleen D. Holland, W.D.N.Y.. docs.t: Judge Colleen D. Holland (W.D.N.Y.) — Junior lawyers
docs.x: Judge Colleen D. Holland, W.D.N.Y.. Junior lawyers: The court strongly encourages letting junior lawyers examine witnesses at trial and hearings and argue motions. Where the court is inclined to rule on the papers, a representation that a junior lawyer will argue weighs in favor of holding oral argument, and the court will entertain reasonable requests for a senior lawyer to supplement the argument.

docs.t: Judge Leslie G. Foschio (W.D.N.Y.) — Deposition guidelines: objections and instructions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Leslie G. Foschio, W.D.N.Y.. Deposition guidelines: objections and instructions (trap): The judge’s Guidelines for Discovery Depositions are so ordered in every civil case and enforced on motions. At the start, deposing counsel must instruct the witness to ask deposing counsel, not the witness’s own counsel, for any clarification, and the witness must comply. Objections are preserved and must not be made during the deposition, except those waived if not made under Fed. R. Civ. P. 32(d)(3)(B) and those needed to assert a privilege, enforce a court-ordered limitation on evidence, or present a Rule 30(d) motion. Objections must be succinct, state only the basis, and not suggest an answer. Counsel may not instruct or ask a witness not to answer unless counsel has objected on privilege or a court-ordered limitation on evidence.

Any such conference, permitted or not, must be noted on the record by the participating counsel, with its purpose and outcome, and deposing counsel may inquire into it to find out whether there was witness coaching.

docs.t: Judge Leslie G. Foschio (W.D.N.Y.) — Deposition guidelines: documents and questioning
docs.x: Judge Leslie G. Foschio, W.D.N.Y.. Deposition guidelines: documents and questioning: Deposing counsel must give the witness’s counsel a copy of every document shown to the witness, either before the deposition or as each document is shown. The witness and counsel have no right to discuss documents privately before the witness answers questions about them. One question at a time; let the witness answer fully without interruption; no characterization of or comment on answers. If an answer seems unresponsive, say so and have the stenographer repeat the question; if a question is unclear, the examiner may rephrase or withdraw it. No argument between counsel over objections or the nature of questions; note the objection on the record and seek relief after the examination. Avoid unnecessary on-the-record recitation or lengthy quotation of documents.

docs.t: Judge J. Daniel Breen (W.D. Tenn.) — Rule 16(b) scheduling order (trap)
docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Rule 16(b) scheduling order (trap): The judge’s form sets separate joinder and amendment deadlines for plaintiff and defendant, plus dates for each side’s Rule 26 expert disclosures, Rule 26(e) supplementation, written discovery, depositions, and dispositive motions. Absent good cause, the dates won’t be modified or extended. Motions to compel must be filed and served within 45 days of the default or of service of the response, answer, or objection at issue, unless extended for good cause; otherwise the objection to the default or response is waived. Final Rule 26(a)(3) witness and exhibit lists are due on set dates for each side, with a set number of days to object. The joint pretrial order, jury instructions, and motions in limine share a single due date, and the order fixes the pretrial conference and trial dates.

docs.t: Judge J. Daniel Breen (W.D. Tenn.) — Court’s track scheduling forms
docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Court’s track scheduling forms: The page also posts the court’s Standard, Expedited, and Complex Track forms (for example, standard track: discovery closes 300 days after service on the first defendant; Daubert motions 15 days and dispositive motions 30 days after the close). They restate L.R. 7.2 (proposed orders to the judge’s ECF mailbox, consultation before non-Rule 12/56/59/60 motions, leave for other replies within 7 days) and allow a reply on Rule 12 and 56 motions within 14 days (L.R. 12.1(c), 56.1(c)).

docs.t: Judge J. Daniel Breen (W.D. Tenn.) — Voir dire
docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Voir dire: The judge asks standard questions first (trial length, case knowledge, ties to counsel, parties, and witnesses, prior jury and litigation experience, ability to follow the law, disabilities), then lets counsel conduct additional voir dire before marking challenges. In criminal cases the court also asks about law-enforcement employment; jurors answering yes about criminal-matter involvement (or, in drug cases, drug experiences) come forward to discuss it at the bench with court and counsel.

docs.t: Judge J. Daniel Breen (W.D. Tenn.) — Preliminary instructions
docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Preliminary instructions: Jurors are told they may take notes, which stay in the jury room overnight. Openings are described as an outline, not evidence or argument; in criminal cases the defense may, but need not, open.

docs.t: Judge J. Daniel Breen (W.D. Tenn.) — Standard civil charge
docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Standard civil charge: The court’s civil charge covers general duties, preponderance, expert, deposition, and interrogatory evidence, note use, stipulations, compensatory, punitive (malicious, wanton, or oppressive conduct, assessed separately for each defendant, and only after unanimous actual or nominal damages), and nominal damages (a token sum such as $1.00, not combined with compensatory damages). A copy of the instructions goes to the jury room. The deliberation charge includes language encouraging a verdict and asking jurors in the minority to reconsider, without surrendering honest convictions.

docs.t: Judge J. Daniel Breen (W.D. Tenn.) — Standard criminal charge
docs.x: Judge J. Daniel Breen, W.D. Tenn.. Standard criminal charge: The criminal charge tracks the Sixth Circuit pattern numbering (e.g., 2.01A multiple counts, 7.02B defendant’s testimony, 7.03 expert testimony) and includes forms for judicial notice of venue, stipulations (including a prior-felony stipulation), law-enforcement witnesses, and the indictment. The verdict form goes to the jury in a folder that is returned to the marshal during breaks. Jury notes go through the marshal, and jurors must not disclose their numerical division.

Emergency motions: also email the motion and supporting papers to the ECF Inbox, copying all counsel. Expedited motions must be captioned as expedited and state the reasons. A Notice of Settlement triggers an automatic order denying pending motions without prejudice as moot. docs.x: Judge Mark Saalfield Norris Sr., W.D. Tenn.. Non-jury cases: proposed findings and conclusions 2 weeks before trial. Trial briefs are encouraged but not required in jury trials.

docs.t: Judge Mark Saalfield Norris Sr. (W.D. Tenn.) — Trial

Stand to address the court or object; only one attorney per witness; no examination beyond redirect and recross except in exceptional circumstances. Give the deputy notice of videotaped testimony on or before the final pretrial conference. No formal motion to admit exhibits is needed; move them individually around when presented.
